explanation: The Get-Up-and-Go test is a quick, practical way to evaluate a patient's balance, sit-to-stand transition, and walking stability. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h3)

question: On which side of the body should a patient hold a single-point walking cane?

options.A: Alternating hands with every step
options.B: Always in the dominant hand
options.C: The weak side of the body
options.D: The strong side of the body

explanation: Holding the cane on the strong side allows the patient to lean weight onto the device while moving the weaker leg forward. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h4)

question: A patient using axillary crutches complains of numbness and tingling in their fingers. What instruction should the nurse provide?

options.A: Switch immediately to using a standard four-wheeled walker
options.B: Adjust the crutches so they fit higher up in the armpit
options.C: Lean your upper body forward to relieve hand pressure
options.D: Support your body weight on your hands, not your armpits

explanation: Resting body weight on the armpits compresses nerves and blood vessels, leading to nerve damage and tingling; weight must go through the hand grips. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h4)

question: What is the primary safety item a nurse should place around a patient's waist before assisting with a transfer?

options.A: A standard leather belt
options.B: A soft restraining strap
options.C: A gait belt
options.D: An elastic binder

explanation: A gait belt gives the nurse a safe, secure handhold to support the patient without pulling on their clothing or arms. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h5)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to keep a wide stance and bend their knees when lifting or moving a patient?

options.A: To increase upper body muscular strength instantly
options.B: To prevent the patient from feeling nervous or unsteady
options.C: To ensure the patient can place their feet flat on the floor
options.D: To lower the center of gravity and protect the back

explanation: Proper body mechanics with a wide base of support reduces strain on the nurse's lumbar spine during physical maneuvers. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h5)

question: How often should a bedbound patient ideally be repositioned to prevent pressure injuries?

options.A: Only when the patient complains
options.B: Once every twelve hours
options.C: At least every two hours
options.D: Once per day during the morning shift

explanation: Turning or repositioning a patient every two hours relieves continuous pressure on vulnerable skin areas and tissues. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h6)

question: Which complication is most directly linked to sluggish blood flow in the legs of an immobile patient?

options.A: Orthostatic hypotension
options.B: Deep vein thrombosis
options.C: Peripheral neuropathy
options.D: Pulmonary edema

explanation: Immobility slows venous return from the lower extremities, which allows blood clots to form more easily in deep veins. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h6)

question: Which of the following is a common home hazard that frequently leads to patient falls?

options.A: Bright lighting in bedroom hallways
options.B: Grab bars installed inside showers
options.C: Low-pile wall-to-wall carpeting
options.D: Loose scatter rugs on slick floors

explanation: Loose rugs easily slip underfoot or catch assistive device tips, making them a major tripping hazard in homes. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h7)

question: A patient with unsteady balance prepares for discharge home. What is the best nursing action to address home safety?

options.A: Discuss removing tripping hazards and installing bathroom grab bars
options.B: Advise the patient to remain in bed until fully recovered
options.C: Recommend replacing all furniture with hospital-grade equipment
options.D: Suggest wearing thick socks for warmth and comfort while walking

explanation: Practical modifications like clearing walkways and adding bathroom grab bars directly prevent falls in the living environment. [learn more](GNS324_U3_T8#GNS324_U3_T8_h7)

question: Why is visiting a patient's home so helpful for disease management?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for any medications.
options.B: It guarantees that the patient will never need a hospital visit.
options.C: It allows nurses to observe real-world habits and living conditions.
options.D: It places the entire workload on family members instead.

explanation: You get a true picture when you see where patients actually live! Home care lets you spot daily habits and environmental factors that directly affect their health.

question: How does home care primarily change the way healthcare is delivered?

options.A: From hospital-centered interventions to daily life
options.B: From professional nursing to family-only treatment
options.C: From chronic disease management to acute surgery
options.D: From everyday living to rigid facility schedules

explanation: Instead of keeping care locked inside hospital walls, home nursing brings support directly into the patient's personal living space.

question: Which of these is a great example of primary prevention in the home?

options.A: Performing range-of-motion exercises for a stroke survivor
options.B: Checking blood sugar levels to find early diabetes
options.C: Giving a seasonal flu vaccine to a healthy client
options.D: Treating an open pressure ulcer on the heel

explanation: Primary prevention stops illnesses before they even start. Giving a vaccine to a healthy person is a classic way to protect them!

question: What is the main goal of tertiary prevention?

options.A: To reduce complications and manage established chronic illnesses
options.B: To prevent a disease from ever occurring in a healthy person
options.C: To screen a population for hidden risk factors
options.D: To cure acute infections using high-dose antibiotics

explanation: Tertiary prevention steps in after a disease is already there—helping patients manage symptoms, avoid complications, and live their best daily life.

question: When checking a home for safety, which of these is a common physical hazard?

options.A: High white blood cell count
options.B: Elevated resting heart rate
options.C: Incorrect medication dosage
options.D: Loose floor rugs

explanation: Watch out for loose rugs! They are physical hazards that easily cause elderly patients to trip and fall at home.

question: A nurse notices a dark hallway and no grab bars in the shower. What type of assessment is this?

options.A: Home environmental safety assessment
options.B: Pharmacological toxicity review
options.C: Tertiary rehabilitation evaluation
options.D: Secondary disease screening

explanation: Spotting physical risks like poor lighting or missing bathroom grab bars is part of a home environmental safety check.

question: What daily measurement is most crucial for a home care patient with heart failure?

options.A: Handgrip strength
options.B: Visual acuity
options.C: Body weight
options.D: Hair growth rate

explanation: Daily weighing is a lifesaver for heart failure patients. It helps catch hidden fluid buildup early before serious breathing problems start.

question: Why is teaching patients to spot early warning signs of their chronic disease so important?

options.A: It completely cures chronic conditions like diabetes.
options.B: It ensures family members take over all nursing duties.
options.C: It stops patients from ever taking prescription drugs.
options.D: It allows for early action before emergency hospitalization is needed.

explanation: When patients recognize small changes early, they can call for help or adjust care before a scary health crisis lands them in the hospital.

question: Which handy tool do home care nurses often use to help patients manage multiple daily pills?

options.A: Sterile wound dressing
options.B: Blood pressure cuff
options.C: Peak flow meter
options.D: Weekly pill organizer

explanation: A weekly pill box is a simple lifesaver! It sorts medications by days and times, helping patients stay on track.

question: Why do many older home care patients struggle to take their medications correctly?

options.A: They have too many extra financial resources.
options.B: Complex dosing schedules cause confusion.
options.C: Doctors always prescribe only one pill per day.
options.D: Medication bottles are always too easy to open.

explanation: When a patient has too many pills with different rules (some before meals, some at bedtime), it gets super confusing. Keeping it simple is key!

question: What is the single most effective way to stop infections from spreading in home care?

options.A: Proper hand hygiene
options.B: Restricting all visitors permanently
options.C: Wearing sterile gowns all day
options.D: Spraying rooms with strong perfumes

explanation: Good old-fashioned handwashing is your best defense! It removes germs and stops them from passing between you and your patients.

question: Which of these is a common myth about infection control in home settings?

options.A: That handwashing helps reduce bacterial spread
options.B: That family members can transmit respiratory viruses
options.C: That the home environment is naturally germ-free
options.D: That used needles require special puncture-proof containers

explanation: Don't be fooled—homes are not naturally sterile! Good cleaning and hygiene habits are still a must everywhere.

question: What is the purpose of using the 'teach-back' method during patient education?

options.A: Asking the patient to repeat instructions in their own words
options.B: Testing the patient on medical history terminology
options.C: Reading a medical textbook aloud to the family
options.D: Having the nurse lecture for an hour without stopping

explanation: Teach-back is brilliant: you ask them to explain your instructions back to you in their own words so you know they truly understand.

question: Why should nurses actively involve family caregivers in disease management education?

options.A: It removes all responsibility from the professional nurse.
options.B: It helps caregivers spot red flags and offer safe daily support.
options.C: It prevents the patient from ever speaking to a doctor.
options.D: It ensures the family takes over financial medical costs.

explanation: Family members are with the patient every day. Training them means someone is always watching for warning signs when you aren't there.

question: Which healthcare professional do home care nurses often team up with to improve patient mobility?

options.A: Hospital security guards
options.B: Pharmaceutical researchers
options.C: Financial accountants
options.D: Physical therapists

explanation: Physical therapists are fantastic partners! They work alongside nurses to help patients build strength, balance, and safely move around at home.

question: What is a key part of emergency preparedness in a home care plan?

options.A: Disconnecting all medical equipment to save electricity
options.B: Waiting for the annual checkup to report severe symptoms
options.C: Knowing who to call and what steps to take during a sudden crisis
options.D: Relying solely on neighbors for medical decisions

explanation: When an emergency strikes, panic shouldn't take over. Having a clear plan of who to call keeps both the patient and family safe.

question: Which part of the brain acts as the emotional alarm system that triggers the fight-or-flight response during anxiety?

options.A: The pituitary gland
options.B: The cerebellum
options.C: The medulla oblongata
options.D: The amygdala

explanation: Spot on! The amygdala is our emotional radar. It processes threats and sounds the alarm early when we feel anxious. You've got this!

question: What is the main job of brain chemicals like GABA and serotonin?

options.A: Controlling voluntary skeletal muscle movement
options.B: Managing red blood cell production in bone marrow
options.C: Increasing body temperature during an infection
options.D: Regulating mood and calming nerve activity

explanation: Great job! GABA and serotonin act like natural brakes in the brain, keeping our mood balanced and our nerves from firing too wildly.

question: To diagnose Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), how long must a patient experience excessive, hard-to-control worry?

options.A: One year
options.B: Six months
options.C: One month
options.D: Two weeks

explanation: Correct! For a GAD diagnosis, the persistent worry needs to span at least six months. Keep up the brilliant study habit!

question: A patient suddenly feels intense terror, chest pain, and a sense of doom that peaks within minutes. What condition matches this?

options.A: Generalized anxiety disorder
options.B: Social anxiety disorder
options.C: Specific phobia
options.D: Panic disorder

explanation: Exactly! Those sudden, terrifying rushes with strong physical signs are classic hallmarks of panic attacks seen in panic disorder.

question: How do tough economic pressures and daily security worries affect mental health at home?

options.A: They completely eliminate the biological risk factors for psychiatric illness
options.B: They permanently alter DNA structure within a single generation
options.C: They create chronic, ongoing stress that depletes psychological resilience
options.D: They exclusively cause short-term physical injuries without mental effects

explanation: Spot on! Constant daily stressors keep our nervous system on edge, wearing down our mental strength over time. You're doing great.

question: Which of these is NOT a common stressor that can worsen anxiety for people living in Nigeria?

options.A: Economic hardship and inflation
options.B: Security challenges and community unrest
options.C: Societal pressures regarding family provision
options.D: Abundant financial surplus and job security

explanation: That's right! Having plenty of money and job security actually lowers stress rather than causing anxiety. Easy peasy!

question: Which physical sign do patients very often report when they are feeling extremely anxious?

options.A: Rapid heartbeat or palpitations
options.B: Sustained lowering of blood pressure
options.C: Uncontrolled weight gain over days
options.D: Permanent loss of skin pigmentation

explanation: Correct! When anxiety hits, adrenaline surges through the body, frequently causing a racing heart or palpitations.

question: Why is it important to run physical medical tests on someone presenting with severe anxiety symptoms?

options.A: To determine the correct dosage of psychotherapy immediately
options.B: To measure the exact concentration of brain neurotransmitters
options.C: To rule out medical conditions like hyperthyroidism that mimic anxiety
options.D: To prove that the patient is faking psychological distress

explanation: Spot on! Conditions like an overactive thyroid can cause a racing pulse and tremors that look just like anxiety. We always check the physical body first!

question: Which group of medications is usually prescribed first for the long-term management of anxiety disorders?

options.A: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs)
options.B: Short-acting skeletal muscle relaxants
options.C: Intravenous corticosteroid therapies
options.D: First-generation antipsychotic medications

explanation: You got it! SSRIs are the go-to choice for long-term anxiety care because they work well and have a safer side-effect profile.

question: Why are benzodiazepines generally prescribed for short-term use only during sudden, severe anxiety?

options.A: They permanently cure the underlying brain chemistry imbalance in one dose
options.B: They stop working entirely after the very first day of administration
options.C: They carry a significant risk of tolerance and physical dependence
options.D: They immediately cause severe permanent organ damage if used at all

explanation: Spot on! The body gets used to benzodiazepines very quickly, which can lead to dependence and addiction if taken for too long.

question: A patient is having a rising panic attack at home. What is the best immediate nursing action?

options.A: Encourage the patient to drink several cups of strong coffee
options.B: Scold the patient for worrying over unimportant matters
options.C: Leave the patient completely alone in a dark room until they calm down
options.D: Guide the patient through slow, deep breathing exercises

explanation: Brilliant! Slow, steady breaths help lower the heart rate and calm down hyperventilation. Nursing care at its finest!

question: How does cutting back on coffee and energy drinks help a patient dealing with an anxiety disorder?

options.A: It prevents central nervous system stimulation that mimics anxiety symptoms
options.B: It guarantees uninterrupted sleep for twelve hours every night
options.C: It acts as a powerful direct replacement for antidepressant medication
options.D: It cures the genetic predisposition linked to panic disorder

explanation: Correct! Caffeine is a stimulant that causes jitteriness and a fast pulse—things you definitely don't need when managing anxiety. Smart choice!

question: What is a frequent risk when people try to self-medicate ongoing, untreated anxiety?

options.A: Substance abuse and dependence
options.B: Sudden permanent loss of vision
options.C: Drastic and rapid skeletal bone growth
options.D: Complete immunity to bacterial infections

explanation: Spot on. Many turn to alcohol or drugs to numb their anxious feelings, which often leads into a struggle with substance dependence.

question: During a home visit, a patient with severe anxiety mentions thoughts of ending their life. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.A: Tell the patient to snap out of it and focus on positive thoughts
options.B: Wait until the next scheduled clinic appointment in two weeks
options.C: Advise the patient to exercise vigorously until exhausted
options.D: Assess the immediate suicide risk and ensure a safe environment

explanation: You nailed it. Safety always comes first. When a patient talks about self-harm, assessing immediate risk is the most crucial step.

question: What is the most common form of dementia seen among older adults?

options.A: Vascular dementia
options.B: Frontotemporal dementia
options.C: Lewy body dementia
options.D: Alzheimer's disease

explanation: You'll see this a lot in clinical practice! Alzheimer's disease accounts for the vast majority of all dementia cases worldwide.

question: How does vascular dementia primarily develop, setting it apart from Alzheimer's disease?

options.A: It only affects physical movement without touching memory
options.B: It is triggered strictly by nutritional deficiencies in old age
options.C: It is caused by reduced blood flow to the brain from problems like strokes
options.D: It develops entirely from sudden viral infections of the nervous tissue

explanation: Spot on! Vascular dementia happens when blood supply to the brain is blocked or reduced—often due to tiny strokes—starving brain cells of oxygen.

question: Which stage of dementia usually lasts the longest and is known for noticeable confusion and wandering?

options.A: Pre-clinical stage
options.B: Early stage
options.C: Middle stage
options.D: Late stage

explanation: The middle stage is typically the longest. It brings clear behavioral changes, like wandering and needing help with daily tasks.

question: A patient with dementia starts forgetting close family members and frequently wanders away. Which stage do these signs point to?

options.A: Middle stage
options.B: Late stage
options.C: Mild cognitive impairment
options.D: Early stage

explanation: Spotting familiar faces becomes tough in the middle stage, and wandering is a classic behavior to watch out for as confusion increases.

question: Why is it important to remove loose rugs from the home of a patient with dementia?

options.A: To keep the house looking neat for visitors
options.B: To stop the patient from eating fabric fibers
options.C: To prevent dangerous tripping and fall accidents
options.D: To reduce dust allergies in the living room

explanation: Safety first! Loose rugs are sneaky slip hazards for older adults whose balance and spatial awareness are already affected.

question: Why do nurses often recommend exit alarms or high door locks for homes with a dementia patient?

options.A: To prevent the patient from wandering outside and getting lost
options.B: To keep uninvited guests from entering the compound
options.C: To punish the patient for bad behavior during the day
options.D: To force the patient to stay inside their bedroom at night

explanation: Wandering can be very dangerous because patients easily get disoriented. Simple environmental barriers keep them safe inside.

question: Why is it better to offer simple, closed choices rather than open-ended questions when talking to a dementia patient?

options.A: It reduces the mental effort required to process and answer the question
options.B: It ensures the patient always drinks water instead of sugary beverages
options.C: It allows the nurse to maintain strict control over the daily routine
options.D: It prevents the patient from changing their mind later in the day

explanation: Think of it like saving phone battery! Open questions can overwhelm a tired or confused brain, whereas 'Would you like tea or water?' is much easier to answer.

question: A patient insists that their mother, who passed away years ago, is coming to visit today. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Argue firmly that the mother is dead to teach them reality
options.B: Scold the family members for not correcting the patient's false memory
options.C: Ignore the comment completely and pretend you did not hear anything
options.D: Acknowledge the feeling behind the statement and gently redirect their attention

explanation: Argueing causes distress. Instead, validate their emotion ('You really miss your mum, don't you?') and gently steer their focus elsewhere.

question: When a dementia patient suddenly acts out or becomes aggressive, what is this most often a sign of?

options.A: A direct side effect of drinking too much water
options.B: A deliberate attempt to upset family members
options.C: An unmet physical need or reaction to distress
options.D: A permanent change in their core personality

explanation: Behavior is communication! When they can't say 'I'm in pain' or 'I'm scared,' they might lash out instead.

question: Which of these is NOT a recommended first step when managing challenging behaviors in dementia?

options.A: Immediate prescription of heavy antipsychotic medications
options.B: Reviewing the daily routine for sources of overstimulation
options.C: Playing soft and familiar background music
options.D: Looking for signs of physical pain or discomfort

explanation: Always start with non-drug approaches! Heavy meds carry serious risks and shouldn't be the first resort for everyday behavioral issues.

question: Why are finger foods often recommended for patients in the middle to late stages of dementia?

options.A: They make eating easier for patients who struggle with utensils
options.B: They eliminate the need for any supervision during meal times
options.C: They guarantee the patient will consume more protein than meat stews
options.D: They prevent the patient from ever dropping crumbs on the floor

explanation: Using forks and spoons can become too complex. Finger foods help patients feed themselves independently and keep up their nutrition.

question: A patient refuses a bath because the bathroom feels cold and confusing. What is the best nursing approach?

options.A: Scold the patient for being uncooperative with personal hygiene
options.B: Cancel all future baths indefinitely to avoid upsetting the patient
options.C: Warm the room, simplify the process, and break it down into gentle steps
options.D: Force the patient into the tub immediately to maintain hygiene standards

explanation: Making the environment cozy and taking things slow helps ease fear and resistance during personal care.

question: What exactly is caregiver burnout?

options.A: A state of physical, emotional, and mental exhaustion from long-term caregiving
options.B: A sudden financial profit gained from running a home care agency
options.C: A formal medical diagnosis of dementia given to family members
options.D: A temporary feeling of tiredness after cleaning the house

explanation: Caregiving is heavy work. Burnout happens when looking after a loved one drains all physical and emotional energy without enough rest.

question: Why can cultural stigma surrounding dementia make things especially tough for families in Nigeria?

options.A: It guarantees that traditional healers will cure the underlying brain damage
options.B: It forces the government to provide free nursing homes in every state
options.C: It eliminates all forms of physical illness in elderly community members
options.D: It can cause families to hide the affected relative and isolate themselves from support

explanation: Stigma creates shame and secrecy, which stops families from reaching out for the healthcare advice and community support they need.

question: What is a bone fracture?

options.A: A stretching injury to skeletal muscle fibers
options.B: A severe infection inside the bone marrow
options.C: A complete tearing of a ligament near a joint
options.D: A break or disruption in the continuity of a bone

explanation: Simple and clear! A fracture just means the bone's structure has cracked or broken. You've got this!

question: Why is a home health nurse so important after a patient goes home with a broken bone?

options.A: To prescribe stronger narcotic pain medications when healing slows down
options.B: To monitor ongoing recovery and prevent long-term immobility complications
options.C: To perform immediate open reduction surgery inside the patient's home
options.D: To replace the hospital surgeon during routine follow-up visits

explanation: Most healing happens outside the hospital. Home nurses are vital for catching early warning signs and helping patients recover safely at home.

question: Which type of fracture happens when the broken bone pushes through the skin?

options.A: Comminuted fracture
options.B: Closed fracture
options.C: Open fracture
options.D: Greenstick fracture

explanation: When bone breaks through the skin, it's called an open (or compound) fracture. This requires extra care because of the high risk of infection!

question: Why are greenstick fractures much more common in young children than in adults?

options.A: Children have much higher calcium levels in their bones.
options.B: Children experience lower impact forces during play.
options.C: Children's bones lack a periosteum protective layer.
options.D: Children's bones are softer and more flexible.

explanation: Kids' bones are still growing, so they tend to bend and splinter on one side like a fresh green twig rather than snapping completely.

question: In a neurovascular check for a injured limb, what does the letter 'P' stand for?

options.A: Pulselessness
options.B: Pressure
options.C: Perforation
options.D: Pruritus

explanation: Think of the 5 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, and Paralysis. They help us quickly spot nerve and blood flow issues!

question: A patient with a new leg cast says their toes feel very numb and tingly. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Perform a complete neurovascular assessment and report findings
options.B: Massage the toes gently to restore normal local blood circulation
options.C: Elevate the leg above heart level and encourage deep breathing
options.D: Administer a prescribed oral sleeping pill to calm the patient

explanation: Numbness and tingling are red flags for trapped nerves or poor blood flow. Checking thoroughly and reporting right away keeps the patient safe.

question: What is the main goal of fracture reduction?

options.A: To permanently increase the overall length of the injured limb
options.B: To dissolve any blood clots that formed around the injury site
options.C: To completely eliminate the need for any pain medication
options.D: To restore the broken bone fragments back into proper anatomical alignment

explanation: Reduction simply means putting the broken bone ends back in their correct place so they can heal straight and strong.

question: Why is careful pin-site care so important for a patient with an external fixator?

options.A: To encourage faster bone mineralization around the pin insertion sites
options.B: To prevent bacteria from traveling down the metal pins into the bone
options.C: To stop the external metal frame from rusting over time
options.D: To prevent the skin from sticking permanently to the metal frame

explanation: Since the pins go through the skin, they create a pathway for germs. Keeping them clean stops nasty deep bone infections like osteomyelitis!

question: When handling a wet plaster cast, why should nurses use the palms of their hands instead of their fingertips?

options.A: To stop the wet plaster material from sticking permanently to skin
options.B: To prevent indentations that can cause pressure sores on the skin
options.C: To prevent the nurse from getting skin irritation from chemicals
options.D: To make sure the heavy cast does not crack before it dries

explanation: Fingertips leave deep dents in wet plaster. Those little flat spots can press painfully against the skin and cause pressure ulcers later.

question: During a home visit, you notice the weights for a patient's skin traction are resting on the floor. What is your very first action?

options.A: Document that the patient is non-compliant with bedrest orders
options.B: Remove the traction setup entirely because it is no longer effective
options.C: Ensure the weights hang freely without touching the floor or bed
options.D: Add extra weight to make up for the time the weights spent resting

explanation: Traction weights must always hang free! If they touch the floor, the pulling force stops, and the bones won't stay aligned.

question: Where should a patient place their body weight when walking with crutches?

options.A: Through the shoulders
options.B: Against the armpits
options.C: Through the hands
options.D: Against the chest wall

explanation: Always push through the hands, not the armpits! Putting weight in the armpits can damage important nerves and blood vessels.

question: What is the correct gap to keep between the top of the crutch and the patient's armpit?

options.A: Exactly one full hand width
options.B: Five to six finger widths
options.C: Two to three finger widths
options.D: No gap, it should touch firmly

explanation: A 2 to 3 finger-width gap keeps the crutch from pressing into the armpit nerves while the patient walks.

question: Which nutrient is especially helpful for building collagen and healing bones?

options.A: Vitamin K
options.B: Potassium
options.C: Vitamin C
options.D: Sodium

explanation: Vitamin C is a superstar for building collagen—the framework that new bone tissue needs to grow on!

question: Why is checking bowel movements extra important for patients taking opioid pain medications for a fracture?

options.A: Pain medications speed up digestion too much and cause diarrhea.
options.B: Opioids destroy beneficial bacteria living inside the large intestine.
options.C: Opioids frequently cause significant and uncomfortable constipation.
options.D: Pain medications prevent the body from absorbing dietary calcium.

explanation: Opioids slow down the gut big time. Anticipating and preventing constipation is a huge part of keeping patients comfortable during recovery.

question: What is a major sign of compartment syndrome that sets it apart from normal fracture pain?

options.A: Severe pain that is not relieved by prescribed opioid pain medication
options.B: Sharp pain that completely disappears after taking deep breaths
options.C: Mild aching pain that occurs only when the patient stands up
options.D: Gradual itching underneath the cast as the bone begins to heal

explanation: When strong pain meds don't touch the pain at all, think compartment syndrome! It means dangerous pressure is building up inside the muscle.

question: Which complication of long bone fractures (like the femur) involves breathing trouble and a spotty rash?

options.A: Fat embolism syndrome
options.B: Osteomyelitis infection
options.C: Superficial skin breakdown
options.D: Chronic bone spur formation

explanation: Fat droplets from inside the bone marrow can slip into the bloodstream after a long bone break, traveling to the lungs and brain. Watch out for breathing issues and a petechial rash!

question: What is the leading chronic health condition that results in lower limb amputation?

options.A: Rheumatoid arthritis
options.B: Chronic bronchitis
options.C: Essential hypertension
options.D: Diabetes mellitus

explanation: Diabetes damages blood vessels and nerves over time, making wounds hard to heal and often leading to tissue death. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h1)

question: Why does severe peripheral vascular disease often lead to an amputation?

options.A: Blocked arteries prevent oxygen and nutrients from reaching tissues, causing cell death.
options.B: High blood pressure forces the limb to swell until the skin splits open.
options.C: Excess fluid builds up in the muscles and causes the bone to snap.
options.D: Weakened veins allow blood to pool and turn into dangerous blood clots.

explanation: Think of it like a plant without water—when blood flow is cut off, the tissue lacks oxygen and dies, which can create gangrene that requires surgery. Great job learning the basics!

question: What is a transtibial amputation commonly known as?

options.A: Above-knee amputation
options.B: Below-knee amputation
options.C: Partial foot amputation
options.D: Ankle disarticulation

explanation: The tibia is the shin bone, so a transtibial procedure removes the limb below the knee joint. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T12#GNS324_U4_T12_h2)

question: Why would a surgeon leave an amputation wound open instead of stitching the skin right away?

options.A: To allow drainage and prevent trapping severe infection inside the wound
options.B: To stretch the skin flaps so they cover a larger area of bone
options.C: To give the patient time to practice moving the joint before closure
options.D: To make it easier to fit a temporary plastic cast on the bone

explanation: If there's an infection present, closing the skin immediately would trap bacteria inside and cause abscesses. Leaving it open temporarily keeps things safe!

question: What emergency item must always be kept right at the bedside after an amputation surgery?

options.A: A heating pad
options.B: A tourniquet
options.C: An extra pillow
options.D: A bedside commode

explanation: A tourniquet is kept at the bedside just in case there is sudden, heavy bleeding from the surgical site that needs immediate stopping. Safety first!

question: On day one after a below-knee amputation, what should the nurse do to help prevent joint stiffness (contractures)?

options.A: Encourage the patient to cross their legs while sitting up.
options.B: Limit the time the residual limb rests elevated on pillows.
options.C: Apply a heavy sandbag directly over the end of the stump.
options.D: Keep the residual limb propped up on pillows for the entire day.

explanation: Keeping the stump propped up for too long causes the muscles to tighten in a bent position. We want to keep those joints flexible!

question: When wrapping a residual limb with an elastic bandage, where should the pressure be tightest?

options.A: At the bottom end of the stump
options.B: Equally tight all the way up
options.C: Near the top of the joint
options.D: Across the middle portion

explanation: Wrapping tighter at the bottom (distal end) pushes fluid upward and helps shape the limb into a neat cone, which makes fitting a prosthesis much easier later.

question: Why should a patient avoid putting lotion on their residual limb before wearing a shrinker sock?

options.A: Oily substances make the prosthesis slide off during walking exercises.
options.B: Lotion dissolves the elastic fibers inside the special compression bandage.
options.C: Trapped moisture creates a breeding ground for bacteria and skin breakdown.
options.D: Moisturizers stop the surgical incision from closing completely.

explanation: Lotion plus a tight wrap equals a warm, wet space where bacteria and fungi love to grow. Keeping the skin clean and dry prevents rashes and breakdown!

question: What is the main difference between phantom limb sensation and phantom limb pain?

options.A: Pain only happens during the day, while sensation occurs exclusively while sleeping.
options.B: Sensation means the limb is still there, while pain means the nerve has died completely.
options.C: Pain is purely psychological, while sensation is caused by poor blood flow.
options.D: Sensation involves normal feelings like tingling, while pain involves burning or shooting hurt.

explanation: Phantom sensation is just a harmless awareness that the limb is missing (like feeling an itchy toe), whereas phantom pain is actual uncomfortable, shooting distress.

question: A patient complains of a burning pain in a leg that was surgically removed last week. How should you, as the nurse, respond?

options.A: Acknowledge the pain as real neuropathic discomfort and report it for treatment.
options.B: Tell the patient this feeling is temporary and will vanish within a few hours.
options.C: Suggest that the patient is imagining things because of anxiety over surgery.
options.D: Gently remind the patient that the leg is gone so the pain cannot actually exist.

explanation: Phantom pain is very real! It comes from the cut nerve endings trying to heal, so always validate your patient and get them the relief they need.

question: Which muscle groups need the most strengthening when a patient is learning to use crutches after an amputation?

options.A: Facial and neck muscles
options.B: Small toe flexors
options.C: Lower leg calf muscles
options.D: Upper body and core muscles

explanation: Using crutches without a lower limb means the arms, shoulders, and chest have to do all the heavy lifting. Time for some push-ups!

question: Why is early physical therapy encouraged soon after amputation surgery?

options.A: To stretch the skin until it breaks open for drainage
options.B: To force the brain to stop feeling the missing limb
options.C: To prevent joint stiffness and maintain muscle strength
options.D: To prevent the patient from ever needing a wheelchair

explanation: Getting moving early keeps the joints flexible and stops the muscles from getting weak before it's time for a prosthesis.

question: What emotional reaction do patients very commonly experience right after losing a limb?

options.A: Indifference to physical changes
options.B: Grief and a sense of loss
options.C: Complete memory loss
options.D: Immediate joyful acceptance

explanation: Losing a body part is a huge life change. Patients go through a normal grieving process, and it's our job to support them with empathy.

question: Why is it so helpful for a recovering patient to talk to another person who has also gone through an amputation?

options.A: It stops the patient from ever experiencing phantom limb pain again.
options.B: It gives practical proof that a fulfilling life and independence are possible.
options.C: Friends who share the same diagnosis speed up physical wound healing.
options.D: Peer visitors are trained medical professionals who can change dressings.

explanation: Seeing someone else thrive after the same experience gives wonderful hope and makes the patient feel much less alone.

question: What is the most important home safety change to make in the bathroom after an amputation?

options.A: Replacing all porcelain fixtures with plastic ones
options.B: Removing the bathroom door to improve airflow
options.C: Installing grab bars near the toilet and shower
options.D: Painting the bathroom walls a bright, cheerful color

explanation: Wet bathroom floors plus new mobility challenges spell danger. Grab bars and shower seats keep baths safe and independent!

question: Why should loose throw rugs be removed from a patient's home after surgery?

options.A: They easily slide underfoot and cause dangerous falls.
options.B: They prevent the wheelchair wheels from rolling smoothly.
options.C: They trap moisture and cause the home humidity to rise.
options.D: They block the medical equipment from plugging into the wall.

explanation: Unsecured rugs love to slip on smooth floors, making them a major tripping hazard for anyone learning to get around with new supports.

question: What visual acuity score in the better eye (even with glasses) is generally used to define legal blindness?

options.A: 20/70 or worse
options.B: 20/40 or worse
options.C: 20/100 or worse
options.D: 20/200 or worse

explanation: You've got this! Legal blindness is officially classified as having a corrected visual acuity of 20/200 or lower in the better eye.

question: Why is checking a patient's 'functional vision' so helpful when planning their daily nursing care?

options.A: It shows what the patient can actually see and do in daily life.
options.B: It determines the exact medical cause of the eye disease.
options.C: It changes the official hospital diagnosis code.
options.D: It proves whether the patient needs surgery immediately.

explanation: Brilliant! Functional vision looks at practical everyday abilities rather than just clinical numbers, helping us figure out the best ways to support their independence.

question: Which eye condition mainly causes a loss of straight-ahead or central vision due to damage to the macula?

options.A: Chronic open-angle glaucoma
options.B: Senile cataracts
options.C: Diabetic retinopathy
options.D: Age-Related Macular Degeneration

explanation: Spot on! Age-Related Macular Degeneration specifically targets the macula, affecting the center of a person's visual field.

question: A patient with long-term diabetes complains of blurry vision and dark spots. Which eye problem should you suspect first?

options.A: Acute glaucoma
options.B: Retinal detachment
options.C: Nuclear cataracts
options.D: Diabetic retinopathy

explanation: Well done! Years of high blood sugar can damage the small blood vessels in the retina, making diabetic retinopathy a very common cause of vision changes.

question: What is the best first step when walking into the hospital room of a patient with a visual impairment?

options.A: Stand quietly by the bed until they notice you.
options.B: Touch their shoulder gently to grab their attention.
options.C: State your name and role clearly before approaching.
options.D: Turn on all the room lights to maximum brightness.

explanation: Spot on! Always use your voice first so you don't startle them since they cannot see you enter the room.

question: What medical term is used to describe specific blind spots inside a person's field of vision?

options.A: Cataracts
options.B: Diopters
options.C: Scotomas
options.D: Refractions

explanation: You're learning fast! Scotomas are small or large patches in the visual field where vision is reduced or completely missing.

question: Why is it important to keep furniture in the exact same spot for a patient who has low vision?

options.A: Government housing regulations require fixed furniture setups.
options.B: It prevents the wooden legs from scratching the floor tiles.
options.C: It ensures the air conditioner cools the room evenly.
options.D: They build a mental map of their surroundings to walk safely.

explanation: Exactly right! Keeping things in place lets patients navigate their space confidently from memory without tripping or bumping into things.

question: Which room adjustment helps prevent falls on indoor steps for someone with low vision?

options.A: Removing the handrails to give more space for walking
options.B: Polishing the wooden steps until they are shiny and smooth
options.C: Installing dark-colored carpeting that blends with the floor
options.D: Placing bright, contrasting tape on the edge of each step

explanation: Great job! High-contrast markings make it much easier for the patient's eyes to catch where each step begins and ends.

question: How should you position yourself when using the 'sighted guide' technique to walk with a blind patient?

options.A: Pushing the patient in a wheelchair from behind
options.B: Holding the patient's hand and pulling them along
options.C: Walking slightly ahead with the patient holding your elbow
options.D: Walking directly behind the patient to catch them if they fall

explanation: You got it! Having the patient hold your elbow lets them feel your body movements naturally as you walk together.

question: Which of these actions does NOT help promote independence in a visually impaired patient?

options.A: Teaching them to organize clothing by texture and location
options.B: Doing all of their personal grooming tasks for them to save time
options.C: Encouraging the use of a white cane for outdoor travel
options.D: Suggesting talking clocks and large-print books

explanation: Spot on! Doing everything for them actually takes away their independence and confidence. We want to support them in doing what they can!

question: How should you respond if a newly diagnosed visually impaired patient feels angry, sad, or hopeless?

options.A: Inform them that crying will only make their eye pressure worse
options.B: Tell them to stop worrying because things could be much worse
options.C: Acknowledge and validate their feelings as a normal part of grieving
options.D: Change the subject immediately to avoid upsetting them further

explanation: Wonderful nursing instinct! Losing vision is a huge life change, and validating their emotions helps them process the grief and move toward healing.

question: What is a major benefit of connecting a visually impaired patient with a peer support group?

options.A: Diagnosing the underlying cause of their eye disease
options.B: Providing free medical treatments and prescription drugs
options.C: Sharing practical coping strategies and reducing isolation
options.D: Replacing the need for professional nursing home care

explanation: Spot on! Talking to others going through similar experiences helps patients feel less alone and gives them great everyday tips for living with low vision.

question: What does profound deafness mean for a patient?

options.A: Complete absence of auditory input
options.B: Ability to hear loud noises only
options.C: Painful sensitivity to normal sounds
options.D: Temporary loss of hearing function

explanation: Think of profound deafness as a total lack of hearing input. Because of this, normal speech can't be processed, even with hearing aids.

question: How is being 'hard of hearing' different from profound deafness?

options.A: Hard of hearing always requires immediate surgical intervention
options.B: Hard of hearing individuals retain some residual hearing capacity
options.C: Deafness is always caused by an infection in the outer ear
options.D: Deaf individuals can still understand whispered conversations easily

explanation: Patients who are hard of hearing still have some hearing left (residual hearing). This means devices like hearing aids can help them a lot!

question: Which part of the inner ear turns sound vibrations into electrical signals for the brain?

options.A: Cochlea
options.B: Tympanic membrane
options.C: Malleus
options.D: Auditory canal

explanation: The cochlea is shaped like a little snail shell. It is packed with fluid and tiny hair cells that translate physical sound waves into nerve impulses.

question: What is the main job of the three tiny bones in the middle ear?

options.A: Produce cerumen to trap foreign bodies
options.B: Amplify and transmit sound vibrations
options.C: Drain excess fluid from the inner ear
options.D: Maintain balance and body posture

explanation: Meet the malleus, incus, and stapes! They take the vibrations from your eardrum, boost their volume, and pass them deeper into the ear.

question: What usually causes conductive hearing loss?

options.A: Blockages or problems in the outer or middle ear
options.B: Degeneration of hair cells in the cochlea
options.C: Inability of the brain to process sounds
options.D: Damage to the vestibulocochlear nerve

explanation: Conductive hearing loss simply means something is physically blocking sound waves from traveling through the outer or middle ear—like earwax or fluid.

question: A patient has damage to their cochlea and auditory nerve. What type of hearing loss is this?

options.A: Sensorineural hearing loss
options.B: Central processing loss
options.C: Mixed hearing loss
options.D: Conductive hearing loss

explanation: When the inner ear structures (like the cochlea) or the hearing nerve itself are damaged, we call it sensorineural hearing loss.

question: Which group of medications is well-known for damaging hearing (ototoxicity)?

options.A: H2 receptor antagonists
options.B: Aminoglycoside antibiotics
options.C: Short-acting nitrates
options.D: Inhaled corticosteroids

explanation: Watch out for aminoglycoside antibiotics! They can sometimes harm the inner ear and lead to hearing problems if not monitored closely.

question: An older patient seems to be losing their hearing, but it's actually a simple, fixable blockage. What is it?

options.A: Cerumen impaction
options.B: Cochlear hair cell death
options.C: Tympanic membrane scarring
options.D: Auditory nerve atrophy

explanation: Cerumen impaction is just a fancy word for heavy earwax buildup! Once you clean it out, the patient's hearing usually pops right back to normal.

question: What quick, easy test can you perform right at the bedside to check a patient's hearing?

options.A: Electroencephalogram
options.B: Computed tomography scan
options.C: Whispered voice test
options.D: Complete blood count

explanation: The whispered voice test is a fast, free, and easy bedside screening tool to check if a patient can hear soft sounds.

question: Why would a doctor order a tympanometry test?

options.A: To test the patient's balance and coordination
options.B: To check middle ear function and detect fluid
options.C: To measure the electrical activity of the brain
options.D: To visualize the tiny bones of the inner ear directly

explanation: Tympanometry tests how well your eardrum moves when air pressure changes. It's great for spotting fluid or pressure issues behind the eardrum.

question: How do cochlear implants work differently from standard hearing aids?

options.A: They only amplify sound in the outer ear
options.B: They are used exclusively for conductive loss
options.C: They require no external power source
options.D: They directly stimulate the auditory nerve

explanation: While regular hearing aids just make sounds louder, cochlear implants completely bypass damaged parts of the ear and zap electrical signals straight to the auditory nerve!

question: You are talking to a patient with profound hearing loss. What is the very first thing you should do to help them understand you?

options.A: Rely entirely on telephone calls for follow-up
options.B: Face the patient directly and ensure good lighting
options.C: Turn on the television to keep the room comfortable
options.D: Speak in a very loud voice from across the room

explanation: Always face your patient and make sure the room is well-lit so they can read your lips and pick up on your facial expressions.

question: What is a very common emotional challenge for people dealing with untreated hearing loss?

options.A: Improved cognitive processing
options.B: Heightened sense of euphoria
options.C: Increased physical strength
options.D: Social isolation and depression

explanation: When it's hard to hear conversations, people often start pulling away from social gatherings, which can lead to loneliness and depression.

question: How can you best support a newly diagnosed hearing-impaired patient who feels lonely and isolated?

options.A: Connecting the patient with local support groups and rehabilitation
options.B: Limiting family visits to reduce communication fatigue
options.C: Focusing solely on medical treatments without addressing feelings
options.D: Telling the patient to avoid all social gatherings permanently

explanation: Connecting them to support groups and rehab programs helps them realize they aren't alone and teaches them awesome new ways to communicate.

question: What do we call it when cancer cells break away and spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymph system?

options.A: Apoptosis
options.B: Mitosis
options.C: Metastasis
options.D: Hyperplasia

explanation: You've got this! Metastasis is simply the word for when cancer travels from its original spot to start new tumors elsewhere. Great job!

question: How are benign tumors different from malignant ones?

options.A: Benign tumors cannot grow larger than a few millimeters.
options.B: Benign tumors only occur in the blood and lymphatic system.
options.C: Benign tumors do not invade nearby tissues or spread to distant sites.
options.D: Benign tumors consist of dead cells rather than dividing cells.

explanation: Think of benign tumors as staying put in one place without invading surrounding tissues. They aren't cancerous like malignant ones!

question: Which major category of cancer starts in the skin or the lining of internal organs?

options.A: Leukemias
options.B: Lymphomas
options.C: Carcinomas
options.D: Sarcomas

explanation: Carcinomas are the most common type of cancer because they begin in the epithelial tissues that line our skin and organs. Keep pushing forward!

question: Which type of cancer starts in the bone marrow and doesn't form solid lumps or tumors?

options.A: Melanoma
options.B: Sarcoma
options.C: Leukemia
options.D: Carcinoma

explanation: Leukemia affects our blood-forming tissues, sending lots of abnormal white blood cells into circulation instead of forming a solid tumor.

question: What is the single biggest cause of cancer worldwide that we can actually prevent?

options.A: Processed meat intake
options.B: Alcohol consumption
options.C: Ultraviolet radiation
options.D: Tobacco use

explanation: Tobacco smoke contains harmful chemicals that damage our DNA. Avoiding tobacco is one of the best health choices anyone can make!

question: Which viral infection is strongly linked to causing cervical cancer in women?

options.A: Human immunodeficiency virus
options.B: Human papillomavirus
options.C: Epstein-Barr virus
options.D: Hepatitis B virus

explanation: High-risk strains of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) can cause cellular changes over time, which is why screening and vaccines are so important.

question: What is often one of the very first warning signs of internal cancers like stomach or pancreatic cancer?

options.A: Unexplained weight loss
options.B: High fever and chills
options.C: Severe joint swelling
options.D: Sudden visual impairment

explanation: When growing tumors change the body's metabolism and steal nutrients, rapid, unexpected weight loss can happen. Good clinical awareness!

question: A patient shows you a skin mole that has recently changed color and grown irregularly. What should you do first?

options.A: Refer the patient for a prompt medical evaluation and biopsy.
options.B: Advise the patient to monitor the mole at home for another year.
options.C: Apply a medicated topical steroid cream to mole.
options.D: Reassure the patient that changing moles are always benign.

explanation: Any changing mole or spot needs a professional check-up right away to rule out skin cancer. You are learning to protect your patients!

question: What test is always needed to give a 100% definitive diagnosis of cancer?

options.A: Tissue biopsy
options.B: Complete blood count
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.D: Ultrasound scan

explanation: Scans and blood tests give us great clues, but looking at a tiny tissue sample under a microscope is what confirms cancer for sure.

question: In the TNM cancer staging system, what does the letter 'M' stand for?

options.A: Malignancy grade
options.B: Microscopic size
options.C: Metastasis
options.D: Mitosis rate

explanation: You've got this! In TNM staging, 'M' tells us if the cancer has traveled or metastasized to other parts of the body.

question: Why do patients on chemotherapy often lose their hair and get mouth sores?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs target all fast-growing healthy cells along with cancer cells.
options.B: Chemotherapy directly destroys the nervous system.
options.C: Chemotherapy causes severe dehydration in mucosal tissues.
options.D: Chemotherapy blocks the absorption of essential vitamins.

explanation: Chemo attacks rapidly dividing cells—not just cancer cells, but also normal ones like hair roots and mouth linings. That's why these side effects happen!

question: What is the main goal of using radiation therapy in cancer treatment?

options.A: Cleansing the entire circulatory system of loose circulating tumor cells
options.B: Providing systemic relief from widespread metastatic bone pain
options.C: Using targeted high-energy rays to destroy cancer cells in a specific area
options.D: Stimulating the bone marrow to produce extra infection-fighting white blood cells

explanation: Radiation is a localized treatment. It uses powerful beams aimed precisely at the tumor to zap those cancer cells while sparing healthy tissue.

question: A patient on chemotherapy calls the clinic saying their temperature is 38.5°C. What should you tell them to do?

options.A: Drink plenty of cold fluids and monitor the temperature for another day.
options.B: Apply a cool damp cloth to the forehead to bring down the fever.
options.C: Take a dose of paracetamol and rest in bed until tomorrow morning.
options.D: Come to the hospital immediately for a medical evaluation and blood work.

explanation: Fever in a chemo patient is an emergency because their immune system is low. Quick action can save a life!

question: Why should cancer pain medication be given on a regular schedule rather than only when the patient asks?

options.A: It ensures the prescription bottle lasts for the full prescribed month.
options.B: It prevents the patient from developing a physical addiction to the drugs.
options.C: It maintains a steady blood level of medication to prevent severe pain from returning.
options.D: It reduces the risk of experiencing common gastrointestinal side effects.

explanation: Scheduled dosing keeps pain under control before it gets too intense. It's much easier to prevent pain than to chase it once it spikes!

question: When can palliative care start for someone diagnosed with cancer?

options.A: At the time of diagnosis alongside curative treatment
options.B: Only when all chemotherapy and radiation have failed
options.C: Strictly during the final twenty-four hours of life
options.D: Only after the patient is discharged to hospice care

explanation: Palliative care isn't just for the end of life—it can start right away to help manage symptoms and keep the patient comfortable while fighting the disease.

question: What is the primary focus of nursing care for a cancer patient receiving end-of-life support?

options.A: Testing new experimental medication regimens
options.B: Maximizing comfort and maintaining dignity
options.C: Restoring normal nutritional and metabolic status
options.D: Aggressively treating the underlying tumor growth

explanation: At the end of life, our nursing focus shifts completely to surrounding the patient and family with comfort, peace, and dignity.

question: What does the top number in a blood pressure reading represent?

options.A: Systolic pressure when the heart rests
options.B: Systolic pressure when the heart beats
options.C: Diastolic pressure when the heart rests
options.D: Diastolic pressure when the heart beats

explanation: The top number is the systolic pressure, which measures the force in the arteries when the heart contracts or beats. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h1)

question: Why is hypertension frequently described as a silent condition?

options.A: It causes severe pain only at night
options.B: It only affects people who cannot speak
options.C: It disappears on its own without treatment
options.D: It damages blood vessels without causing early symptoms

explanation: High blood pressure often develops over years without any noticeable warning signs, which is why regular checks are necessary. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h1)

question: What is the term for high blood pressure that has no single identifiable medical cause?

options.A: Primary hypertension
options.B: Malignant hypertension
options.C: Gestational hypertension
options.D: Secondary hypertension

explanation: Primary or essential hypertension makes up the vast majority of cases and develops gradually from lifestyle and genetic factors. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h2)

question: A patient asks why their salt intake matters so much for their blood pressure. What is your best response?

options.A: Salt stops your kidneys from producing urine completely.
options.B: Salt directly destroys your heart muscle cells over time.
options.C: Extra salt makes your body hold onto extra water, which pushes harder against your artery walls.
options.D: Salt causes your blood vessels to instantly expand and burst.

explanation: Sodium causes fluid retention, increasing the total volume of blood circulating and raising the pressure inside the vessels. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h2)

question: What happens to a blood pressure reading if the cuff used on the patient's arm is too small?

options.A: It remains completely normal
options.B: It reads falsely high
options.C: It reads falsely low
options.D: It drops to zero

explanation: A cuff that is too small requires more pressure to compress the artery, resulting in an artificially elevated reading. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h3)

question: How long should a patient rest quietly before having their blood pressure measured?

options.A: Exactly 30 seconds
options.B: At least 5 minutes
options.C: No rest is needed
options.D: At least 1 hour

explanation: A short resting period ensures that recent physical activity or rushing does not falsely elevate the blood pressure reading. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h3)

question: What is the primary focus of the DASH diet for managing high blood pressure?

options.A: Eating plenty of fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy while reducing sodium
options.B: Eliminating all carbohydrates completely from daily meals
options.C: Eating only raw meat and root vegetables
options.D: Drinking large amounts of herbal teas and liquid supplements

explanation: The DASH diet emphasizes nutrient-dense whole foods and mineral-rich produce while cutting back on salt and unhealthy fats. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h4)

question: Why does regular aerobic exercise help lower blood pressure over time?

options.A: It thickens the walls of the arteries permanently.
options.B: It removes all cholesterol from the body immediately.
options.C: It forces the kidneys to stop filtering blood.
options.D: It strengthens the heart muscle so it can pump blood more efficiently.

explanation: When the heart becomes stronger through exercise, it requires less effort to circulate blood, which reduces the pressure on artery walls. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h4)

question: Why do many patients stop taking their blood pressure medication without telling their nurse?

options.A: They feel fine and assume the condition has gone away.
options.B: The medications always cure hypertension within one week.
options.C: Blood pressure pills taste sweet like candy.
options.D: Doctors prefer patients to stop taking pills after a month.

explanation: Because high blood pressure is asymptomatic, patients often mistake feeling well for being cured and abandon their regimen. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h5)

question: Which class of blood pressure medication works primarily by helping the kidneys remove excess water and sodium from the body?

options.A: Diuretics
options.B: Statins
options.C: Antibiotics
options.D: Beta-blockers

explanation: Diuretics, or water pills, prompt the kidneys to excrete sodium and water, reducing overall blood volume and pressure. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h5)

question: What is the main difference between a hypertensive urgency and a hypertensive emergency?

options.A: Urgency always requires immediate surgery, but emergency does not.
options.B: An emergency involves active damage to target organs, while urgency does not.
options.C: Emergency only happens in children, while urgency happens in adults.
options.D: Urgency features readings over 300 mmHg, while emergency is much lower.

explanation: Both feature very high readings, but an emergency is distinguished by acute, ongoing damage to vital organs like the heart or brain. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h6)

question: A patient with a blood pressure of 220/130 mmHg complains of a sudden, blinding headache and confusion. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Encourage the patient to drink a large glass of salty broth.
options.B: Wait two hours to see if the headache goes away on its own.
options.C: Tell the patient to lie down and sleep it off until morning.
options.D: Arrange emergency transport to a hospital immediately.

explanation: Severe blood pressure elevation accompanied by neurological symptoms indicates a hypertensive emergency requiring urgent medical intervention. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h6)

question: How does chronic high blood pressure eventually lead to heart failure?

options.A: It forces the left ventricle to work so hard that the muscle thickens and weakens over time.
options.B: It fills the heart chambers with excess air.
options.C: It shrinks the heart valves until they fall apart.
options.D: It causes the heart to stop beating entirely within a few hours.

explanation: Constantly pumping against high resistance makes the heart muscle enlarge and eventually lose its pumping efficiency, resulting in heart failure. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h7)

question: Which of the following organs is NOT typically considered a primary target organ damaged by long-term hypertension?

options.A: Brain
options.B: Kidneys
options.C: Spleen
options.D: Heart

explanation: The primary target organs damaged by chronic high blood pressure are the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T16#GNS324_U4_T16_h7)

question: Which cells in the pancreas are responsible for producing insulin?

options.A: Alpha cells
options.B: Beta cells
options.C: Delta cells
options.D: Acinar cells

explanation: Insulin is synthesized and secreted by the beta cells located within the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T17#GNS324_U4_T17_h1)

question: What happens in the body when there is not enough insulin or when insulin doesn't work properly?

options.A: Red blood cells destroy circulating nutrients
options.B: The pancreas stops producing digestive enzymes
options.C: Cells rapidly absorb too much sugar
options.D: Glucose accumulates in the bloodstream

explanation: Without enough working insulin, sugar can't get inside your body's cells for energy, so it builds up in your blood (hyperglycemia). You've got this!

question: What is the main underlying cause of Type 1 diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Gradual resistance of muscle cells to insulin
options.B: Severe dietary deficiency of essential vitamins
options.C: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.D: Temporary hormonal changes during pregnancy

explanation: In Type 1 diabetes, the body's immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the insulin-making beta cells in the pancreas. Keep up the great study habit!

question: How is Type 2 diabetes different from Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Type 2 requires immediate lifelong oral medication without dietary changes
options.B: Type 2 is strictly an acute condition that resolves without long-term treatment
options.C: Type 2 only affects elderly patients who have a family history of kidney disease
options.D: Type 2 involves insulin resistance and relative deficiency rather than total destruction

explanation: In Type 2 diabetes, your body still makes insulin, but your cells resist using it properly—unlike Type 1 where the beta cells are completely wiped out. You're learning fast!

question: What is the medical term for the excessive thirst that a diabetic patient often feels?

options.A: Polyphagia
options.B: Polyuria
options.C: Polydipsia
options.D: Paresthesia

explanation: Polydipsia simply means extreme thirst. It happens because the body is losing a lot of water through frequent urination (polyuria). You are building a solid clinical vocabulary!

question: Why do patients with untreated diabetes sometimes experience rapid weight loss?

options.A: Excessive fluid intake flushes away all dietary nutrients
options.B: High blood sugar levels speed up the normal metabolic rate
options.C: Kidneys filter out solid food particles into the urine
options.D: The body breaks down stored fat and muscle for energy

explanation: When glucose can't enter the cells for fuel, the body panics and starts burning its own fat and muscle instead, causing sudden weight loss. Makes total sense when you picture it!

question: Which medication is absolutely essential for a patient living with Type 1 diabetes to survive?

options.A: Metformin
options.B: Acarbose
options.C: Sulfonylurea
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Because Type 1 bodies cannot make insulin, daily insulin replacement is a matter of survival. Another win for your clinical knowledge today!

question: A patient with rapid-acting insulin asks when they should take their injection. What is the best nursing advice?

options.A: Only right before going to sleep at night
options.B: Just before or right at mealtime
options.C: Two hours after finishing the meal
options.D: Once a week on an empty stomach

explanation: Rapid-acting insulin starts working very quickly, so patients take it right as they eat to match the incoming food sugars. Spot on!

question: Which type of food has the most direct and immediate effect on blood sugar levels?

options.A: Pure water
options.B: Carbohydrates
options.C: Dietary minerals
options.D: Healthy fats

explanation: Carbs break down into glucose during digestion, making them the number one food group to watch for blood sugar management. You're cruising through these!

question: Why do dietitians recommend high-fiber complex carbs instead of simple sugars for diabetic patients?

options.A: They stimulate the pancreas to grow new beta cells
options.B: They contain zero calories and cannot be converted into fat
options.C: They slow down digestion and prevent rapid blood sugar spikes
options.D: They completely eliminate the need for any diabetes medication

explanation: High-fiber carbs take longer to digest, giving a nice, steady release of energy rather than sending blood sugar through the roof. Brilliant nursing logic!

question: How does regular physical exercise help lower a person's blood sugar?

options.A: By permanently curing pancreatic beta cell damage
options.B: By destroying excess sugar in the bloodstream
options.C: By increasing insulin sensitivity in muscle cells
options.D: By slowing down overall body metabolism

explanation: Exercise tunes up your muscle cells so they respond better to insulin, helping them pull glucose out of the blood much easier. Keep up the momentum!

question: Why is daily foot care and inspection so crucial for patients with diabetes?

options.A: Daily observation increases blood circulation to the toes
options.B: Sweat buildup guarantees the rapid development of gangrene
options.C: Nerve damage can prevent them from feeling minor cuts or blisters
options.D: Skin color changes indicate the exact blood sugar level

explanation: Diabetes can cause nerve damage (neuropathy) in the feet, meaning minor sores can go unnoticed and turn into major wounds if not checked daily. Essential nursing wisdom!

question: Which of these is a classic example of a microvascular (small blood vessel) complication of diabetes?

options.A: Diabetic retinopathy affecting the eyes
options.B: Peripheral vascular disease in the legs
options.C: Coronary artery disease leading to angina
options.D: Cerebrospinal stroke affecting speech

explanation: Retinopathy damages the tiny, delicate blood vessels in the eyes, which makes it a classic microvascular complication. You're doing great!

question: What is the primary trigger for diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?

options.A: Consuming too much dietary protein in a single sitting
options.B: An allergic reaction to oral anti-diabetic medications
options.C: Severe lack of insulin forcing the body to break down fat rapidly
options.D: Sudden extreme physical exhaustion after heavy exercise

explanation: When insulin is severely lacking, the body burns fat too fast for fuel. This creates acidic waste products called ketones, leading to DKA. You're mastering advanced concepts!

question: What is the ultimate goal of patient education when teaching someone how to care for their diabetes at home?

options.A: Preventing the patient from ever experiencing normal life stress
options.B: Eliminating all future visits to the primary healthcare clinic
options.C: Empowering the patient to safely manage their daily condition
options.D: Ensuring the family takes complete control of medication administration

explanation: Good education gives patients the tools, knowledge, and confidence to take charge of their own health every day. Love to see it!

question: Which teaching style works best when you are educating a patient who was just diagnosed with diabetes?

options.A: Focusing exclusively on severe complications like kidney failure
options.B: Tailoring information to fit the patient's daily routine and lifestyle
options.C: Insisting that they completely change their diet in one single day
options.D: Handing them a complex medical textbook to read overnight

explanation: Teaching works best when it's practical, personalized, and fits smoothly into the patient's real everyday life. Fantastic work finishing this set!

question: Which germ is the main cause of tuberculosis (TB)?

options.A: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.B: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.C: Corynebacterium diphtheriae
options.D: Bordetella pertussis

explanation: TB is caused by a bacterium called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It loves to settle in the lungs! You'll get this easily with practice.

question: How does tuberculosis mostly spread from one person to another?

options.A: Ingestion of unpasteurized dairy products
options.B: Direct contact with contaminated skin lesions
options.C: Inhalation of airborne droplet nuclei
options.D: Sharing eating utensils and drinking cups

explanation: When someone with active TB coughs or sneezes, tiny droplets float into the air. If others breathe them in, they can catch the infection too.

question: What is the key feature of a latent tuberculosis infection?

options.A: The patient has a productive cough and bloody sputum
options.B: The person is asymptomatic and cannot spread the disease
options.C: The bacteria are rapidly multiplying throughout the bloodstream
options.D: Chest X-rays consistently show severe lung cavity destruction

explanation: Latent TB means the germs are sleeping safely inside the body, kept in check by your immune system. The person feels fine and cannot pass it to others.

question: Why does the body form small bumps called granulomas during a TB infection?

options.A: To help transport oxygen across damaged alveolar membranes
options.B: To produce antibodies that neutralize the bacterial toxins
options.C: To wall off and contain the bacteria within the lungs
options.D: To stimulate rapid production of red blood cells

explanation: Think of granulomas as a smart defensive wall built by your immune system to trap the TB germs so they cannot wander around your lungs.

question: Which breathing sign is a classic warning of active pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: A persistent cough lasting longer than three weeks
options.B: Sudden wheezing and severe shortness of breath
options.C: A sharp, barking cough triggered by cold air
options.D: Copious amounts of clear, watery nasal discharge

explanation: Any cough hanging around for more than three weeks should immediately make you think of TB and prompt a check-up!

question: A patient with active tuberculosis usually reports which set of body-wide signs?

options.A: Sudden weight gain, severe headache, and lethargy
options.B: Night sweats, low-grade fevers, and weight loss
options.C: Constipation, blurred vision, and muscle spasms
options.D: High fever, severe joint swelling, and a skin rash

explanation: Active TB drains the body's energy. Classic signs include drenching night sweats, afternoon fevers, and losing weight without trying.

question: What is the main drawback of a positive Mantoux (tuberculin skin) test?

options.A: It cannot distinguish between latent and active infection
options.B: It only works in patients who have never received vaccinations
options.C: It is completely unreliable for diagnosing immunocompromised adults
options.D: It requires laboratory analysis of blood within two hours

explanation: A positive skin test simply means your immune system has seen TB before. It cannot tell if the infection is sleeping (latent) or active.

question: Which test gives the final confirmation that a patient has active lung TB?

options.A: Physical auscultation of bilateral lung sounds
options.B: Routine complete blood count and electrolyte panel
options.C: Measurement of resting blood pressure and pulse rate
options.D: Sputum culture and acid-fast bacilli smear testing

explanation: Checking the patient's sputum for acid-fast bacilli or growing the germs in a lab gives the definitive proof needed to confirm active TB.

question: What is the main goal of Directly Observed Therapy (DOT) for TB patients?

options.A: Reducing the overall financial cost of purchasing prescription drugs
options.B: Eliminating the need for periodic sputum laboratory testing
options.C: Ensuring patients swallow every medication dose to prevent resistance
options.D: Allowing nurses to monitor daily lung function and oxygen saturation

explanation: With DOT, a health worker watches the patient take their drugs. This stops missed doses and prevents drug-resistant TB strains from forming.

question: Why do doctors treat active tuberculosis with several drugs at once instead of just one?

options.A: To counteract the severe sedative side effects of rifampin
options.B: To prevent the bacteria from developing drug resistance
options.C: To speed up the healing process so drugs are only taken for days
options.D: To completely eliminate normal flora in the gastrointestinal tract

explanation: Hitting TB bacteria with multiple drugs makes it super hard for them to mutate and survive. Multi-drug therapy is a lifesaver!

question: What type of mask must nurses wear when walking into an active TB patient's room?

options.A: Standard paper surgical mask for fluid splashes
options.B: Particulate respirator such as an N95 mask
