options.C: Cloth face covering made from thick cotton fabric
options.D: Plastic face shield with no respiratory filter

explanation: Because TB travels on tiny air particles, ordinary surgical masks won't cut it. An N95 respirator keeps healthcare workers safe!

question: Which simple home practice helps cut down the spread of airborne TB?

options.A: Keeping the patient bedroom door tightly locked at all times
options.B: Using chemical disinfectants to wipe down furniture daily
options.C: Washing all patient eating utensils in boiling water
options.D: Opening windows frequently to ensure good room ventilation

explanation: Fresh air is a powerful ally! Opening windows blows away and dilutes airborne TB germs so others don't breathe them in.

question: Which vitamin is often given alongside isoniazid to protect a patient's nerves?

options.A: Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3)
options.B: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
options.C: Ascorbic Acid (Vitamin C)
options.D: Tocopherol (Vitamin E)

explanation: Isoniazid can drain Vitamin B6 levels, leading to tingling or nerve pain. Adding Vitamin B6 prevents this pesky side effect.

question: Why must patients finish their full course of TB drugs even after they start feeling better?

options.A: The body needs time to rebuild depleted stomach lining cells
options.B: Health authorities require written proof of finishing all pills
options.C: Stopping early causes immediate permanent liver failure
options.D: Remaining bacteria can multiply and cause drug-resistant relapse

explanation: Feeling better doesn't mean all germs are gone. The toughest ones are still hiding and will bounce back stronger if treatment stops early.

question: What is a normal and harmless effect of rifampin that nurses should warn patients about?

options.A: Bright green coloration of saliva and fingernails
options.B: Permanent yellow tinting of the skin and eye sclera
options.C: Orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, and tears
options.D: Severe darkening of the skin on the hands and feet

explanation: Rifampin naturally dyes body fluids a reddish-orange color. It looks alarming, but it's completely normal and harmless!

question: Which anti-TB drug requires regular checks on a patient's vision and color sight?

options.A: Pyrazinamide
options.B: Isoniazid
options.C: Rifampin
options.D: Ethambutol

explanation: Ethambutol can affect eye health (optic neuritis). Regular eye checks help catch any vision changes early before they become serious.

question: How would you best describe depression in a clinical setting?

options.A: A temporary lack of vitamins causing physical weakness
options.B: A minor behavioral adjustment issue in older adults
options.C: A serious mood disorder affecting thoughts and daily activities
options.D: A temporary emotional reaction to physical fatigue

explanation: Spot on! Depression isn't just a brief bad mood or fatigue; it's a true mood disorder that impacts a person's entire daily life and well-being.

question: Why is it important for nurses to look beyond purely physical complaints when checking for depression?

options.A: Patients will always directly report feeling sad without prompting
options.B: Physical complaints always disappear once mental health improves
options.C: Depression frequently presents itself disguised as chronic pain or fatigue
options.D: Physical symptoms are completely unrelated to psychological health

explanation: Great job! Patients often show up with body aches, headaches, or extreme tiredness rather than saying they feel sad. Staying alert to this helps us catch what's really going on.

question: Which type of depression tends to happen during specific times of the year, especially the cold winter months?

options.A: Seasonal affective disorder
options.B: Postpartum depression
options.C: Major depressive disorder
options.D: Persistent depressive disorder

explanation: You got it! Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) kicks in during certain seasons, usually when daylight gets shorter in the winter.

question: How is persistent depressive disorder different from major depressive disorder?

options.A: It affects only new mothers following childbirth
options.B: It only occurs during the winter months of the year
options.C: It is a chronic, milder form lasting for two years or longer
options.D: It lasts for exactly two weeks before disappearing entirely

explanation: Spot on! Persistent depressive disorder hangs around for a long time—two years or more—even if the daily symptoms are a bit milder than major depression.

question: Which chemical messengers in the brain play a major role in mood and depression?

options.A: Serotonin and norepinephrine
options.B: Insulin and glucagon
options.C: Thyroxine and calcitonin
options.D: Sodium and potassium

explanation: Well done! Serotonin and norepinephrine are key neurotransmitters that help regulate our mood. An imbalance here is a big part of why depression happens.

question: A patient is dealing with loneliness and money troubles after losing their partner. What do these life events represent?

options.A: Genetic and chromosomal mutations
options.B: Environmental and situational stressors
options.C: Primary endocrine abnormalities
options.D: Congenital brain structural defects

explanation: You nailed it! Things happening in a person's surroundings—like loss, isolation, or financial stress—are situational triggers that can spark depression.

question: Why do nurses use standard screening tools like the Patient Health Questionnaire in clinical practice?

options.A: To quantify and measure depression symptom severity
options.B: To measure blood levels of neurotransmitters
options.C: To test physical strength and muscular endurance
options.D: To diagnose specific neurological brain disorders

explanation: Exactly! Screening tools give us a clear, structured way to score how severe a patient's depressive symptoms are so we can track their progress.

question: Why should nurses actively ask patients about their mood instead of waiting for them to bring it up?

options.A: Patients with depression lose the ability to speak completely
options.B: Hospital policy forbids patients from mentioning sadness first
options.C: Many patients keep feelings hidden due to social stigma
options.D: Physical assessments replace the need for verbal interviews

explanation: Spot on! Because society often judges mental health issues, many patients hide their pain. Asking gently and directly lets them know it's safe to talk.

question: A depressed patient says that life feels completely hopeless. What is the best, most therapeutic way to reply?

options.A: It sounds like you are carrying a very heavy burden right now. Let us talk about it.
options.B: Do not worry about it, many people feel much worse than you do.
options.C: Everything will look much brighter tomorrow once you get some sleep.
options.D: You have so many things to be grateful for, so try not to feel down.

explanation: Wonderful! Validating their feelings without dismissing them builds trust and opens the door for a truly helpful conversation.

question: Why is it helpful to encourage small, manageable daily goals for a patient struggling with severe depression?

options.A: It prevents the patient from feeling overwhelmed by large tasks
options.B: It eliminates the need for any prescribed medication
options.C: It guarantees the patient will return to work immediately
options.D: It cures the chemical imbalance in the brain instantly

explanation: You got it! Depression drains energy. Breaking the day into tiny, doable steps helps patients feel a sense of success without crashing from exhaustion.

question: About how long does it usually take for antidepressant medications to start showing noticeable improvements?

options.A: Two to four weeks
options.B: A few minutes
options.C: Twenty-four hours
options.D: Six months

explanation: Correct! Antidepressants take time to build up in the body. Patients usually need to wait two to four weeks before feeling the real benefits.

question: Why must nurses remind patients never to stop taking their antidepressants all of a sudden?

options.A: Abrupt discontinuation instantly cures the chemical imbalance
options.B: Stopping quickly causes immediate permanent brain damage
options.C: Sudden cessation can trigger withdrawal symptoms and a return of depression
options.D: Patients will develop a physical addiction to the medication

explanation: Spot on! Stopping suddenly can cause uncomfortable withdrawal effects and bring the depression rushing back. Medication always needs to be tapered off safely under medical guidance.

question: What is the most important nursing action when a patient talks about active thoughts of suicide?

options.A: Wait until the next scheduled clinic visit to report it
options.B: Leave the patient alone in a quiet room to reflect
options.C: Maintain constant supervision and provide a safe environment
options.D: Tell the patient to distract themselves with a hobby

explanation: You nailed it! Safety is always priority number one. Keeping a close eye on the patient and removing any hazards keeps them safe during a crisis.

question: Which of these statements is true when it comes to asking a patient directly about suicide?

options.A: Asking directly opens the door for help and does not cause suicidal thoughts
options.B: Nurses should only ask about suicide if the patient brings it up first
options.C: Asking about suicide will plant the idea into a healthy patient's mind
options.D: Direct questioning is discouraged because it increases patient agitation

explanation: Brilliant! Asking directly doesn't put the idea in their head—it actually brings immense relief because it shows you care and understand how much pain they are in.

question: What is the main sign of psychosis in a patient?

options.A: Severe permanent memory loss
options.B: Sudden loss of motor control
options.C: Loss of touch with shared reality
options.D: Extreme physical exhaustion

explanation: You've got this! Psychosis simply means the person has disconnected from reality, often seeing or believing things that others do not share.

question: Why is visiting a patient with psychosis at home so helpful for a nurse?

options.A: It guarantees complete medication compliance without supervision.
options.B: It provides an entirely stress-free environment foregra the client.
options.C: It eliminates the need for any professional medical intervention.
options.D: It allows the nurse to observe daily environmental triggers.

explanation: Spot on! Seeing patients in their natural home environment helps you spot what stressors around them might be affecting their mental state.

question: How would you describe a delusion?

options.A: A complete lack of emotional expression
options.B: A fixed, false belief resistant to logic
options.C: A sudden inability to speak any words
options.D: A sensory experience without external stimuli

explanation: Well done! A delusion is a strong belief that stays stuck in the person's mind, even when clear facts show it isn't true.

question: A patient hears voices when no one is around. What do we call this?

options.A: Delusion
options.B: Flight of ideas
options.C: Hallucination
options.D: Concrete thinking

explanation: Great job! Hearing things that aren't actually there is an auditory hallucination. Keep up the good work!

question: Which brain chemical is most closely linked to psychotic symptoms?

options.A: Histamine
options.B: Insulin
options.C: Dopamine
options.D: Thyroxine

explanation: You nailed it! Too much activity in the brain's dopamine pathways is a major factor in psychosis.

question: Which of these is NOT a common trigger for a psychotic episode?

options.A: Using recreational cannabis
options.B: Experiencing severe life stress
options.C: Having a family history of psychosis
options.D: Eating a high-sodium diet

explanation: Spot on! Eating salty food won't cause psychosis, but heavy stress, genetics, and substances like cannabis definitely can.

question: What is the main goal of doing a mental status examination during a home visit?

options.A: To measure the client's physical strength and reflexes
options.B: To test the client's long-term memory from childhood
options.C: To evaluate the current cognitive and psychological functioning of the client
options.D: To diagnose the exact subtype of personality disorder

explanation: You got it! The mental status exam gives us a quick, structured snapshot of how the patient is thinking and behaving right now.

question: A community nurse visits a patient with psychosis who looks very suspicious and guarded. What is the best first move?

options.A: Start with calm, non-threatening social conversation before asking clinical questions
options.B: Confront the client about their false beliefs right away to establish reality
options.C: Immediately demand a urine sample to check for illicit drug use
options.D: Leave the home immediately without assessing to avoid agitation

explanation: Brilliant! Taking it slow and building a friendly rapport helps lower anxiety so the patient feels safe enough to talk.

question: Why do many patients with psychosis stop taking their antipsychotic drugs at home?

options.A: Pharmacies give out free drugs
options.B: Doctors prefer short-term use only
options.C: Unpleasant side effects
options.D: The medication cures the disease permanently

explanation: Spot on! Dealing with side effects like weight gain or feeling sluggish is tough, and it's the number one reason patients stop their meds.

question: How do long-acting injectable antipsychotics make community care easier?

options.A: They can be administered without any medical professional present
options.B: They completely eliminate all possible side effects of the medication
options.C: They remove the need for daily pill-taking and ensure steady medication levels
options.D: They cure the underlying genetic cause of the psychotic disorder

explanation: You're doing great! Injectables save patients from swallowing pills every single day and keep their drug levels nice and steady.

question: How should a nurse respond when a patient talks about a frightening delusion?

options.A: Tell the client that police are on their way to arrest them
options.B: Argue aggressively until the client admits the belief is false
options.C: Acknowledge the emotional distress without validating the false belief
options.D: Ignore the statement completely and change the subject

explanation: Well done! Show empathy for how scary the feeling is, but don't agree with the unreal belief. It keeps trust strong!

question: You are trying to calm an upset patient in their living room. Which action keeps everyone safe?

options.A: Touching the client's shoulder frequently to show physical warmth
options.B: Maintaining a safe distance and keeping the exit route clear
options.C: Raising the voice to ensure the client hears every single instruction
options.D: Standing directly in front of the doorway to block the client from leaving

explanation: Spot on! Giving personal space and making sure nobody feels trapped is a golden rule for safety during de-escalation.

question: What does 'caregiver burden' mean in community mental health?

options.A: The physical weight of medical equipment kept inside the home
options.B: The physical, emotional, and financial strain experienced by family caregivers
options.C: The mandatory training hours required to become a certified nurse
options.D: The legal responsibility of paying for all hospital admission bills

explanation: You got it! Looking after a loved one with chronic illness at home can take a heavy toll physically and emotionally.

question: Why is it so important for community nurses to connect families with respite care?

options.A: To fulfill mandatory paperwork requirements for insurance
options.B: To give caregivers temporary relief and prevent burnout
options.C: To punish families who fail to give medications on time
options.D: To permanently remove the client from the family home

explanation: Brilliant! Respite care gives hardworking families a much-needed break so they can recharge and stay healthy too.

question: What is the main goal of psychiatric rehabilitation for a patient with psychosis?

options.A: To restore social, vocational, and independent living skills
options.B: To keep the client admitted inside a hospital indefinitely
options.C: To replace all medications with herbal supplements
options.D: To eliminate the need for any human contact

explanation: Well done! Rehabilitation is all about helping patients rebuild their skills so they can live meaningful, independent lives in the community.

question: Why is spotting early warning signs so important in a relapse prevention plan?

options.A: It guarantees that the client will never experience symptoms again
options.B: It proves that the client is fully cured of the mental illness
options.C: It allows for early intervention before a full psychotic crisis develops
options.D: It gives the insurance company a reason to stop funding home visits

explanation: Spot on! Catching small changes early—like trouble sleeping or rising anxiety—lets us step in before things turn into an emergency.

question: What does the word 'palsy' mean in relation to cerebral palsy?

options.A: Infection of the spinal cord
options.B: A sudden loss of consciousness
options.C: Weakness or problems using muscles
options.D: Gradual shrinking of the brain

explanation: Palsy specifically refers to a lack of muscle control or weakness that interferes with normal movement. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why is cerebral palsy described as a non-progressive condition?

options.A: Symptoms always improve steadily without any medical care
options.B: Treatment can completely repair the damaged brain tissue
options.C: The original brain injury does not get worse over time
options.D: The child will eventually outgrow all physical symptoms

explanation: While the physical body changes and challenges may evolve as a child grows, the underlying brain damage remains static. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h1)

question: Which infant condition involves high bilirubin levels that can cause brain damage and lead to cerebral palsy?

options.A: Kernicterus
options.B: Birth asphyxia
options.C: Placental abruption
options.D: Infant meningitis

explanation: Kernicterus occurs when severe neonatal jaundice goes untreated, allowing bilirubin to cross into the brain and cause permanent injury. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h2)

question: Why are very premature babies with low birth weight at a higher risk of developing cerebral palsy?

options.A: Fragile blood vessels in the immature brain easily rupture and bleed
options.B: Premature babies automatically have defective muscle tissue from birth
options.C: The lungs fail to develop, which immediately starves the heart of oxygen
options.D: Infant formulas lack the essential fats required for nerve growth

explanation: Preterm babies have very delicate blood vessels in their brains that can easily bleed, which can damage the surrounding brain tissue. Great insight for your clinical postings!

question: Damage to which part of the brain is primarily responsible for the balance and coordination problems seen in ataxic cerebral palsy?

options.A: Brainstem
options.B: Basal ganglia
options.C: Motor cortex
options.D: Cerebellum

explanation: The cerebellum is the main brain structure that regulates balance, posture, and coordinated movement. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h3)

question: A child with cerebral palsy presents with very stiff muscles and hyperactive reflexes. Which type of cerebral palsy is this child most likely experiencing?

options.A: Ataxic
options.B: Dyskinetic
options.C: Flaccid
options.D: Spastic

explanation: Spastic cerebral palsy is marked by increased muscle tone and exaggerated reflexes because of injury to the motor cortex or pyramidal tracts. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h3)

question: At what age might a nurse suspect a motor issue if an infant consistently prefers using only one hand?

options.A: By one month of age
options.B: Only during school age
options.C: Before eighteen months
options.D: Around three years old

explanation: Babies usually don't show a strong hand preference early on. Showing one-sided preference before 18 months can be an early sign of hemiplegic cerebral palsy.

question: A 10-month-old cannot sit unsupported, keeps fists clenched, and has stiff legs that cross like scissors when lifted. What should you suspect?

options.A: Normal infant development
options.B: A mild viral ear infection
options.C: Cerebral palsy
options.D: Iron deficiency anemia

explanation: Delayed sitting, tight fists, and scissoring legs are classic signs that point towards cerebral palsy during developmental checks.

question: Which diagnostic imaging tool is most commonly used to identify structural brain abnormalities in a child with suspected cerebral palsy?

options.A: Abdominal ultrasound
options.B: Electrocardiogram (ECG)
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
options.D: Standard chest X-ray

explanation: An MRI provides detailed images of brain tissue, helping clinicians identify areas of past injury or malformation. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h5)

question: Why are regular developmental check-ups by a nurse so important during a baby's first year?

options.A: It replaces the need for any laboratory blood tests or physical examinations
options.B: It proves whether the parents caused the infant's developmental injuries
options.C: It accurately predicts the exact adult height the child will eventually reach
options.D: It helps catch early signs of neurological delays so interventions can start promptly

explanation: Catching delays early lets therapy start when a baby's brain is still developing rapidly and can adapt best!

question: Which healthcare professional primarily helps a child with cerebral palsy learn how to perform daily living tasks like eating and dressing independently?

options.A: Respiratory therapist
options.B: Physical therapist
options.C: Speech pathologist
options.D: Occupational therapist

explanation: Occupational therapists specialize in helping patients develop fine motor skills needed for everyday activities and self-care. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is a major goal of physical therapy in the long-term management of a child with spastic cerebral palsy?

options.A: Eliminating the need for any assistive devices by age five
options.B: Preventing joint contractures and improving functional mobility
options.C: Permanently stopping all involuntary muscle contractions
options.D: Curing the underlying brain lesion through intense exercise

explanation: Physical therapy uses stretching, strengthening, and positioning to keep muscles pliable and prevent permanent joint tightening. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h6)

question: What is the main purpose of recommending respite care to a family caring for a child with severe cerebral palsy?

options.A: To give primary caregivers temporary relief from daily caregiving duties
options.B: To permanently transfer legal custody of the child to the hospital
options.C: To teach the child how to live independently in an apartment
options.D: To provide intensive physical therapy without the parents present

explanation: Respite care gives parents a much-needed break to rest and recharge, helping prevent caregiver burnout.

question: Why should nurses check on the emotional well-being of brothers and sisters in a family affected by cerebral palsy?

options.A: Parents usually ignore the affected child to focus entirely on healthy siblings
options.B: Siblings must legally take over financial caregiving once they turn eighteen
options.C: Siblings are at high risk of developing cerebral palsy themselves
options.D: Siblings can experience feelings of neglect, stress, or added responsibilities

explanation: A chronic condition affects the whole household. Siblings often need emotional support to handle changing roles and big feelings.

question: Which of the following is NOT a common long-term musculoskeletal complication associated with cerebral palsy?

options.A: Scoliosis
options.B: Joint contractures
options.C: Rheumatoid arthritis
options.D: Hip dislocation

explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune joint disease, not a musculoskeletal complication caused by chronic muscle imbalance from cerebral palsy. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T4#GNS324_U4_T4_h8)

question: What mainly determines whether a person with cerebral palsy will live independently as an adult?

options.A: The severity of the physical impairment and presence of associated cognitive or communication deficits
options.B: The specific month of the year that the original brain injury took place
options.C: The total number of siblings living in the same household
options.D: Whether the infant received physical therapy before turning six months old

explanation: How much independence a person achieves depends mostly on how severely their movement, thinking, and communication are affected by the injury.

question: How would you best describe Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)?

options.A: A degenerative muscular disease
options.B: A lifelong neurodevelopmental condition
options.C: A preventable infectious illness
options.D: A temporary childhood behavioral phase

explanation: You've got this! Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition, meaning it stays with a person throughout their entire life. It's just a different way of experiencing the world.

question: Why do healthcare providers use the word 'spectrum' when talking about autism?

options.A: It measures the exact intelligence level of the patient
options.B: It indicates how quickly the condition can be cured
options.C: It shows that symptoms vary widely in severity and presentation
options.D: It proves the condition changes completely every few years

explanation: Think of a rainbow! The 'spectrum' shows that no two autistic people are exactly alike—they experience traits and challenges in vastly different ways.

question: What are the two core behavioral areas used to understand autism?

options.A: Aggressive outbursts and profound sleepiness
options.B: Social communication challenges and repetitive behaviors
options.C: Hyperactivity and attention deficits
options.D: Memory loss and sudden physical paralysis

explanation: Spot on! Autism is primarily identified by differences in how a person communicates socially, alongside a preference for repetitive routines or movements.

question: An autistic patient gets very upset when you shift their routine by just ten minutes. What core feature does this reaction show?

options.A: An intentional attempt to disrupt the ward
options.B: A sign of sudden memory loss
options.C: A rigid adherence to routines and resistance to change
options.D: A lack of basic physical sensation

explanation: It's completely normal for them to feel unsettled here. Predictability brings comfort, so unexpected changes to routines can cause real anxiety.

question: What does 'hypersensitivity' mean in sensory processing for an autistic patient?

options.A: Needing constant loud noises to feel comfortable
options.B: Being easily overwhelmed by normal sights, sounds, or touches
options.C: Being completely unable to feel any physical pain
options.D: Seeking out heavy objects to lift all day

explanation: Great job! Hypersensitive means their nervous system reacts extra strongly to everyday sounds, lights, or textures that others might easily ignore.

question: Why might an autistic patient who is hyposensitive seek out heavy pressure or spin in circles?

options.A: To lower their body temperature during a fever
options.B: To intentionally annoy the healthcare staff on duty
options.C: To practice for athletic events
options.D: To provide their nervous system with the sensory input it craves

explanation: Exactly! When someone is hyposensitive, their nervous system needs extra stimulation—like spinning or deep pressure—just to register the feeling.

question: At what typical ages are toddlers routinely screened for autism using tools like the M-CHAT?

options.A: Around 18 and 24 months of age
options.B: At birth and two weeks old
options.C: During routine adult health checks
options.D: When entering secondary school

explanation: Well done! Screening around 18 and 24 months helps catch developmental differences early so children can get the best support possible.

question: Why should nurses take parents seriously when they worry about their toddler's social development?

options.A: Doctors require parental permission to perform physical exams
options.B: Family concerns are more accurate than formal medical tests
options.C: Parents usually exaggerate normal childhood naughtiness
options.D: Caregivers are often the first to notice early developmental differences

explanation: Parents spend the most time with their little ones and usually spot early warning signs before anyone else walks into the room. Trust their insights!

question: What type of language works best when communicating with an autistic patient?

options.A: Jokes and light sarcasm
options.B: Complex medical terminology
options.C: Fast-paced conversational slang
options.D: Clear and literal language

explanation: You've got it! Autistic individuals often interpret language literally, so keeping your words plain, simple, and direct prevents misunderstandings.

question: You are getting an autistic child ready for a blood draw. What nursing action helps lower their anxiety the most?

options.A: Using a visual schedule to show each step of the procedure
options.B: Talking continuously with complex metaphors about bravery
options.C: Performing the procedure in a brightly lit, busy hallway
options.D: Surprising the child quickly so they do not have time to worry

explanation: Awesome choice! Visual schedules take away the scary unknown by showing pictures of what will happen step-by-step.

question: Why is it so helpful for nurses to involve family caregivers in the care plan for an autistic patient?

options.A: Caregivers know the patient's unique routines and communication cues best
options.B: Caregivers have formal medical degrees in nursing care
options.C: Hospital policy legally requires family members to do the nursing work
options.D: It removes all responsibility from the hospital staff

explanation: Family members are absolute experts on their loved one's specific triggers and favorite comforts. Partnering with them makes all the difference!

question: Which service is especially helpful for giving family caregivers of individuals with ASD a much-needed break?

options.A: Respite care services
options.B: Sudden medication changes
options.C: Mandatory legal arbitration
options.D: Extended hospital admission

explanation: Spot on! Caring for someone full-time is heavy work. Respite care gives families a temporary break to rest and recharge.

question: What is the primary characteristic of a learning disability regarding a person's intelligence?

options.A: Intelligence is generally average or above average
options.B: Intelligence is below the measurable threshold
options.C: Intelligence is severely and globally impaired
options.D: Intelligence fluctuates drastically every day

explanation: People with learning disabilities have normal or high intelligence levels, but their brains process specific types of information differently. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h1)

question: How do learning disabilities differ from global developmental delays?

options.A: Learning disabilities impact every single area of daily physical and mental functioning
options.B: Global delays only appear during adulthood while learning disabilities appear in infancy
options.C: Learning disabilities affect specific academic areas while overall intelligence remains intact
options.D: Global delays are caused exclusively by environmental factors rather than brain function

explanation: Specific learning challenges target isolated skills like reading or math, unlike global delays that affect all areas of development. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h1)

question: Which learning disability specifically impairs a person's ability to perform mathematical calculations?

options.A: Apraxia
options.B: Dysgraphia
options.C: Dyslexia
options.D: Dyscalculia

explanation: Dyscalculia is the specific neurological term for difficulties involving numbers and math concepts. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h2)

question: A student struggles heavily with handwriting, spacing words, and holding a pencil firmly. Which condition fits these signs best?

options.A: Dysgraphia
options.B: Dyscalculia
options.C: Aphasia
options.D: Dyslexia

explanation: Dysgraphia directly interferes with the physical and mental processes of writing and putting thoughts onto paper. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h2)

question: What is a major known contributor to the development of learning disabilities?

options.A: Spending too much time playing outdoors
options.B: Eating excessive refined sugar as a toddler
options.C: Lack of strict discipline in the home
options.D: Genetic and hereditary family history

explanation: Learning disabilities often run in families, highlighting a strong genetic link in how the brain develops and processes information. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h3)

question: Which prenatal event is most associated with an increased risk of neurological learning differences?

options.A: Severe oxygen deprivation during delivery
options.B: Taking prescribed prenatal vitamins daily
options.C: Mild morning sickness during the first trimester
options.D: A pregnant mother eating a high-protein diet

explanation: Perinatal complications like oxygen shortage can disrupt normal brain development, leading to later learning difficulties. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h3)

question: Which sign is commonly seen in school-aged children with an undiagnosed learning disability?

options.A: Total loss of voluntary motor movement
options.B: Complete inability to recognize family members
options.C: Sudden blindness occurring only at night
options.D: Persistent reading errors and letter reversals

explanation: School-aged children typically show signs through ongoing struggles with reading, spelling, and academic tasks. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h4)

question: An adult patient consistently struggles with time management, meeting deadlines at work, and organizing written reports despite being very intelligent. What is a likely underlying cause?

options.A: A sudden onset of a degenerative memory disease
options.B: Severe vitamin deficiency causing temporary confusion
options.C: Deliberate refusal to follow workplace guidelines
options.D: Adult manifestations of an unrecognized learning disability

explanation: Adults with learning disabilities often struggle with executive function tasks like organization, time management, and written expression. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of developmental screening tools used by nurses?

options.A: To replace formal psychological testing in schools
options.B: To flag children who need a comprehensive evaluation
options.C: To provide an immediate and final medical diagnosis
options.D: To measure the exact intelligence quotient score

explanation: Screening tools are meant to identify warning signs early so specialists can perform formal, in-depth assessments. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h5)

question: Why is listening to parental concerns so critical during a nursing developmental assessment?

options.A: Parents can accurately prescribe educational therapies
options.B: Parents hold medical degrees that speed up diagnosis
options.C: Parents often notice subtle discrepancies in daily functioning first
options.D: Parents are legally required to sign all diagnostic tests

explanation: Caregivers spend the most time observing their children and frequently spot early behavioral or learning red flags before anyone else. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h5)

question: Which of the following is an example of an assistive technology used for learning disabilities?

options.A: Standard surgical forceps
options.B: Intravenous infusion pumps
options.C: Digital blood pressure cuffs
options.D: Text-to-speech software

explanation: Assistive technologies like text-to-speech programs help individuals bypass reading barriers to access written content. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h6)

question: A nurse is teaching a parent how to help their child complete homework without getting overwhelmed. What strategy is best to recommend?

options.A: Force the child to finish everything in one long session
options.B: Break large assignments into smaller, manageable steps
options.C: Ignore the homework struggles so the child learns independently
options.D: Punish the child whenever a mistake is made on paper

explanation: Breaking tasks down reduces cognitive overload and anxiety for children who struggle with processing large amounts of information. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h6)

question: How can a learning disability affect other children in the family?

options.A: Siblings may experience feelings of neglect or added stress
options.B: Siblings automatically develop the exact same learning disability
options.C: Siblings lose all of their academic abilities
options.D: Siblings are completely unaffected by the situation

explanation: Family dynamics shift when one child requires extensive attention and advocacy, which can impact brothers and sisters emotionally. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h7)

question: What is the most effective nursing action when supporting stressed parents of a newly diagnosed child?

options.A: Focus only on the child and ignore parental emotional health
options.B: Tell them to stop worrying because children always outgrow it
options.C: Connect them with local parent support groups and active listening
options.D: Advise them to change schools immediately without investigation

explanation: Emotional support and peer connections help parents cope with the challenges of navigating a new diagnosis. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h7)

question: Which professionals are typically part of the multidisciplinary team for a child with a learning disability?

options.A: Cardiologists, physiotherapists, and dietitians only
options.B: Radiologists, lab technicians, and hospital accountants
options.C: Nurses, educational psychologists, and speech therapists
options.D: Surgeons, pharmacists, and hospital administrators only

explanation: A collaborative team approach involves health and educational specialists working together to support the child's specific needs. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h8)

question: What is a key role of the nurse when working with community resources for special needs in Nigeria?

options.A: Diagnosing psychiatric disorders without professional consultation
options.B: Passing strict laws to penalize families who hide children at home
options.C: Connecting families to available local support services and reducing stigma
options.D: Building private special education schools using hospital funds

explanation: Nurses serve as advocates and liaisons, helping families find help in their communities while fighting against societal stigma. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T6#GNS324_U4_T6_h8)

question: In conductive hearing loss, what is the main issue preventing sound from being heard clearly?

options.A: Hair cells inside the cochlea are permanently destroyed
options.B: The auditory nerve is completely severed from the brain
options.C: Sound waves are blocked from reaching the inner ear
options.D: Electrical signals bypass the brain's temporal lobe

explanation: You've got this! Conductive hearing loss simply means something is blocking sound waves from traveling through the outer or middle ear. Think of it like a blocked pathway.

question: Why does sensorineural hearing loss often make speech sound muffled instead of just quiet?

options.A: Excess earwax completely fills the inner ear chambers
options.B: The middle ear bones fuse together to block high pitches
options.C: The eardrum becomes too thick to vibrate at any frequency
options.D: Inner ear damage alters how sound clarity and frequencies are processed

explanation: Great job thinking this through! When the inner ear or auditory nerve gets damaged, it messes up how details and frequencies are sent to the brain, turning clear words into a muffled sound.

question: What is the medical term for natural, age-related hearing loss?

options.A: Otosclerosis
options.B: Barotrauma
options.C: Tympanitis
options.D: Presbycusis

explanation: Spot on! Presbycusis is just the natural wear-and-tear on our hearing as we grow older, usually starting with high-pitched sounds.

question: An older adult suddenly reports muffled hearing in one ear. What simple cause should you check for first?

options.A: A ruptured tympanic membrane from aging
options.B: Permanent damage to the auditory nerve
options.C: Impacted earwax blocking the canal
options.D: Degeneration of the cochlear hair cells

explanation: Always look for the simplest, most treatable cause first! A buildup of earwax (cerumen) is super common and easy to fix.

question: How should a nurse properly perform a whisper test to check a patient's hearing?

options.A: Inspect the deep ear canal with an otoscope to check for active infection
options.B: Whisper numbers and letters while standing slightly behind the patient
options.C: Shout loudly from across the room to test maximum volume tolerance
options.D: Use a tuning fork directly placed on the center of the patient's forehead

explanation: You got it! Standing behind them stops them from reading your lips, giving you an accurate test for each ear on its own.

question: Why is shouting directly at someone with hearing loss often a bad idea?

options.A: Shouting causes immediate physical pain inside the damaged middle ear bones
options.B: Raising your voice increases the pitch into a frequency range that is hard to understand
options.C: Loud sounds trigger defensive reflexes that close the outer ear canal completely
options.D: High volumes permanently destroy the remaining healthy hair cells in the cochlea

explanation: Makes sense, right? When we shout, our voice pitch goes up. Since age-related hearing loss usually steals high pitches first, shouting just makes your words sound more distorted, not clearer!

question: What is the main job of a standard hearing aid?

options.A: To amplify surrounding sounds so the damaged ear can detect them
options.B: To convert spoken words directly into written text on a screen
options.C: To remove impacted earwax from deep inside the ear canal
options.D: To surgically replace the cochlea with an electronic processor

explanation: Exactly! Think of a hearing aid as a tiny personal amplifier that makes everyday sounds loud enough for the ear to pick up.

question: Why are flashing lights and visual alert systems helpful for patients with severe hearing loss?

options.A: They provide visual warnings for home safety hazards that sounds might miss
options.B: Flashing lights help regenerate damaged hair cells inside the inner ear
options.C: They replace the need for regular hearing aid battery replacements
options.D: Bright lights automatically adjust the volume of household televisions

explanation: Brilliant! Since they might miss audio cues, flashing lights for doorbells or smoke alarms help keep them safe at home.

question: What is the best way to start talking to a patient who has a hearing impairment?

options.A: Stand behind the patient and speak loudly to surprise them into listening
options.B: Turn on the television to provide background noise for a normal atmosphere
options.C: Get the patient's attention visually and face them directly before speaking
options.D: Keep the room dark so the patient can concentrate entirely on sound

explanation: You're a natural! Facing them and getting their attention first lets them use your facial expressions and lip movements to understand you better.

question: Why are patients with significant hearing loss also at a higher risk for accidental falls?

options.A: Hearing aids pull the head to one side and throw off normal body alignment
options.B: Inner ear structures involved in hearing also help control balance and spatial orientation
options.C: Patients with poor hearing refuse to wear shoes with proper non-slip soles
options.D: The medication used to treat hearing loss causes sudden daytime sleepiness

explanation: Spot on! The inner ear doesn't just handle hearing—it also houses our balance system. When there's an ear issue, balance can take a hit too.

question: How can untreated hearing loss in an older adult be easily misunderstood by family or caregivers?

options.A: As an early sign of a developing physical movement disorder
options.B: As cognitive decline or depression due to social withdrawal
options.C: As a temporary side effect of common eye drop medications
options.D: As a deliberate attempt to ignore medical instructions

explanation: Right on target. When patients pull back from chats because conversation is exhausting, others sometimes mistake their quietness for confusion or depression.

question: What is a very common emotional reaction for someone dealing with new or worsening hearing loss?

options.A: Sudden aggressive behavior toward healthcare staff
options.B: Uncontrollable euphoria and hyperactivity
options.C: Complete indifference to their personal safety
options.D: Feelings of social isolation and frustration

explanation: Spot on. Finding it hard to talk with loved ones naturally brings frustration and can make someone want to withdraw from social gatherings.

question: What is the primary characteristic of a visual disability?

options.A: Any mild eye infection treated with antibiotic drops
options.B: Total loss of hearing alongside failing sight
options.C: Temporary blurriness caused by eye strain
options.D: Permanent vision loss not corrected by standard glasses

explanation: Visual disability specifically refers to lasting impairment that remains even after standard medical or optical corrections like eyeglasses are applied. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T8#GNS324_U4_T8_h1)

question: How does visual disability generally affect a person's life?

options.A: It prevents individuals from ever communicating verbally
options.B: It interferes with everyday functioning and independent navigation
options.C: It automatically causes complete loss of hearing ability
options.D: It restricts the person to strict bed rest in a hospital

explanation: Because vision is vital for spatial awareness and movement, losing it makes everyday tasks and independent travel challenging. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T8#GNS324_U4_T8_h1)

question: What happens inside the eye of a person with cataracts?

options.A: The natural lens becomes cloudy and blocks clear light
options.B: The macula breaks down and destroys central vision
options.C: Intraocular pressure rises and damages the optic nerve
options.D: Tiny blood vessels on the retina burst and bleed

explanation: Cataracts are characterized by the opacification or clouding of the eye's natural lens, which blurs the incoming light. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T8#GNS324_U4_T8_h2)

question: Which eye condition usually damages side vision first due to a buildup of pressure inside the eyeball?

options.A: Glaucoma
options.B: Diabetic retinopathy
options.C: Macular degeneration
options.D: Cataracts

explanation: Glaucoma happens when pressure builds up inside the eye, slowly damaging the optic nerve. It usually starts by affecting the outer or side vision first. You've got this!

question: Which chart is commonly used in the clinic to test a patient's eyesight?

options.A: Tonometer
options.B: Snellen chart
options.C: Audiometer
options.D: Ophthalmoscope

explanation: The Snellen chart is the classic eye chart with rows of letters that get smaller and smaller. It's the standard tool nurses and doctors use to check visual acuity!

question: Which of the following statements about legally blind individuals is true?

options.A: Most retain some form of residual vision or light perception
options.B: They cannot hear or speak normally compared to others
options.C: They experience total pitch darkness without any exceptions
options.D: Their condition can always be cured with minor surgery

explanation: Legal blindness is a definition for benefits and care, but very few people with this status see absolute blackness; most have usable light or shape awareness. [learn more](GNS324_U4_T8#GNS324_U4_T8_h3)

question: What is the very first thing you should do when walking up to a patient who has a visual impairment?

options.A: Turn off all room lights to protect their sensitive retinas
options.B: Speak clearly, state your name and role, and avoid sudden touch
options.C: Ask a family member to answer all the health questions
options.D: Gently grab their arm to guide them to the examination bed

explanation: Always announce yourself before touching a patient with vision loss. It prevents startling them and helps build a trusting nurse-patient relationship right away.

question: An older adult with severe cataracts is admitted to the ward for a routine hernia repair. What is the most important nursing action during admission?

options.A: Insist that the patient read and sign all consent forms independently
options.B: Keep the room doors locked to prevent wandering
options.C: Remove all personal belongings to create a sterile environment
options.D: Orient the patient carefully to the physical layout of the hospital room

explanation: Helping a patient with low vision learn where things are in a new room (like the bed, bathroom, and call button) keeps them safe and prevents accidental falls.

question: Why is keeping furniture in the same place important for someone with low vision?

options.A: It prevents dust from accumulating under heavy chairs
options.B: It ensures compliance with local fire safety regulations
options.C: It improves natural lighting inside the living space
options.D: It helps them navigate safely using their memory of the layout

explanation: When furniture stays put, individuals can use their memory of the room to walk around safely without bumping into unexpected obstacles.

question: Which simple home modification helps a visually impaired person see the edges of stairs more easily?

options.A: Removing handrails to encourage independent balance
options.B: Polishing the wooden stairs until they shine brightly
options.C: Placing soft carpets over every single step
options.D: Applying high-contrast tape to the edge of each step

explanation: Using bright, high-contrast tape on stair edges makes each step stand out clearly, greatly reducing the risk of a nasty fall.

question: What is the main purpose of a long white cane for mobility?

options.A: To detect ground-level obstacles and uneven surfaces ahead
options.B: To measure the exact distance between walls in a room
options.C: To provide a sturdy walking frame for lower body weakness
options.D: To signal healthcare workers to administer eye medications

explanation: Think of the white cane as an extra helper that sweeps the floor ahead, warning the user about curbs, steps, and obstacles in their path.

question: How do modern smart-speaker voice assistants help someone with severe vision loss?

options.A: They completely restore damaged optic nerves over time
options.B: They allow hands-free control of timers, reminders, and information
options.C: They serve as physical walking canes inside the house
options.D: They automatically administer prescribed glaucoma eye drops

explanation: Voice assistants are wonderful tools! They let users set alarms, check the weather, and make calls just by speaking, bypassing the need to read a screen.

question: What is the clock-face method used for during mealtime assistance?

options.A: Measuring the exact caloric content of each food portion
options.B: Describing the spatial location of food items on a plate
options.C: Checking the temperature of hot liquids before serving
options.D: Timing how fast the patient finishes eating their meal

explanation: The clock-face method (e.g., 'your rice is at 6 o'clock and chicken at 12 o'clock') helps visually impaired patients locate their food and eat independently.

question: You are serving lunch to a patient who is legally blind. What is the best way to help them eat independently?

options.A: Leave the room and let the patient figure out the tray
options.B: Feed the patient spoonful by spoonful to save time
options.C: Mix all the food together so it is easier to scoop up
options.D: Describe the layout of the food using the clock-face method

explanation: Giving a quick guide using the clock-face method empowers patients to feed themselves with dignity and confidence.

question: Why should family caregivers avoid overprotecting a visually impaired relative?

options.A: Overprotection can rob the patient of remaining independence and confidence
options.B: Hospitals require relatives to stay away during recovery
options.C: The patient's eyesight might deteriorate faster with too much help
options.D: Family members will run out of money if they help too much

explanation: Doing everything for a patient can make them feel helpless and depressed. Encouraging them to do what they can builds their confidence!

question: Which emotional response is a patient most likely to show after being told they have permanent vision loss?

options.A: Grief and frustration as they adjust to the change
options.B: Total indifference with no emotional reaction at all
options.C: Immediate excitement to learn new computer skills
options.D: Excessive hunger and sudden weight gain

explanation: Losing one's sight is a major life-changing event. It is completely normal for patients to feel grief, frustration, and sadness as they process the news.

question: What is the main cause of an ischemic stroke?

options.A: High pressure inside the skull
options.B: A ruptured blood vessel in the brain
options.C: A temporary lack of oxygen in the lungs
options.D: A blood clot blocking a brain vessel

explanation: Spot on! An ischemic stroke happens when something blocks blood flow in a brain vessel, cutting off oxygen. You've got this!

question: Why is a transient ischemic attack (TIA) such an important medical warning?

options.A: It always causes permanent paralysis on one side of the body
options.B: It serves as a critical warning sign for a potential major stroke
options.C: It requires immediate surgical removal of brain tissue
options.D: It indicates that the patient has fully recovered their cardiovascular health

explanation: Even though TIA symptoms go away fast, think of it as a loud warning bell that a bigger stroke might be coming!

question: If a patient has a stroke in the left side of the brain, which side of the body will usually show weakness?

options.A: Both sides equally
options.B: The left side
options.C: Only the lower extremities
options.D: The right side

explanation: Remember how nerve pathways cross over in the brainstem? Damage on the left side of the brain affects the right side of the body!

question: What is a classic sign of left-sided neglect after a right-hemisphere stroke?

options.A: Complaining constantly about severe pain in the left arm
options.B: Refusing to speak complete sentences during a conversation
options.C: Exhibiting extreme caution and fear before attempting to walk
options.D: Unintentionally ignoring food, objects, and people on their left side

explanation: With left neglect, the brain literally fails to register the left side of the world. They aren't ignoring you on purpose—their brain just misses that side!

question: When helping a stroke patient with left-sided weakness put on a button-down shirt, which arm goes in first?

options.A: Whichever arm the patient prefers
options.B: The left arm
options.C: The right arm
options.D: Both arms at the same time

explanation: Always dress the weak (affected) side first! It makes maneuvering the fabric much easier before the strong arm is tucked in.

question: A family member is feeding a stroke survivor who can actually hold a spoon with an adaptive grip. What should you do?

options.A: Recommend switching the patient entirely to liquid nutritional supplements
options.B: Praise the family member for providing thorough and efficient care
options.C: Insist that the nurse take over all feeding duties moving forward
options.D: Encourage the patient to use the adaptive spoon independently during meals

explanation: We always want to cheer patients on to do as much as they can for themselves. Independence speeds up recovery!

question: In stroke care, what does 'spasticity' mean?

options.A: Rapid wasting away of muscle tissue
options.B: Complete loss of all muscle sensation
options.C: Uncontrolled trembling during resting states
options.D: Involuntary muscle stiffness and tight spasms

explanation: Spot on! Spasticity is when muscles become tight and stiff because of nerve damage, making them hard to stretch out.

question: Why are range-of-motion exercises so important for a stroke patient with limited movement?

options.A: To reverse the original brain damage caused by the stroke
options.B: To speed up the metabolic rate and prevent weight gain
options.C: To completely eliminate the need for any walking aids
options.D: To prevent painful muscle contractures and joint deformities

explanation: Moving those joints keeps them flexible and stops tight muscles from locking up permanently. Great job!

question: How does expressive aphasia usually show up in a stroke patient?

options.A: Severe shaking of the hands during writing
options.B: Inability to hear sound waves entering the ear
options.C: Total blindness in both visual fields
options.D: Difficulty speaking or finding the right words to say

explanation: With expressive aphasia, the patient usually understands what you're saying, but struggles to get their own words out. Patience is key!

question: What is the best way to talk to a patient who has trouble communicating after a stroke?

options.A: Always finish their sentences if they take longer than two seconds
options.B: Ask simple yes-or-no questions and give them time to answer
options.C: Speak very loudly and quickly to keep their attention focused
options.D: Communicate only through written notes to avoid frustration

explanation: Giving them time and keeping questions simple takes the pressure off and makes chatting much easier.

question: Which nursing action helps prevent deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in a paralyzed leg?

options.A: Keeping the legs elevated above the heart all day
options.B: Massaging the calf muscles vigorously every hour
options.C: Encouraging regular leg movement and compression stockings
options.D: Restricting fluid intake to decrease blood volume

explanation: Movement and compression help keep the blood flowing so it doesn't pool and form dangerous clots! (Never massage a red, swollen calf—that could dislodge a clot!)

question: Why should the head of the bed stay elevated after a stroke patient eats?

options.A: To improve visual focus on surrounding room objects
options.B: To make it easier for the nurse to collect meal trays afterward
options.C: To reduce the risk of food or saliva entering the airway and causing aspiration
options.D: To increase blood pressure and prevent sudden fainting spells

explanation: Gravity is our friend here! Keeping them upright stops food from slipping down the wrong pipe when swallowing muscles are weak.

question: What is the main reason nurses connect family caregivers with respite care services?

options.A: To prevent caregiver burnout and exhaustion
options.B: To reduce the financial cost of home medical equipment
options.C: To permanently transfer legal responsibility for the patient
options.D: To train family members to become licensed nurses

explanation: Looking after a stroke survivor is tough work. Respite care gives families a well-deserved break to rest and recharge!

question: What shows that your discharge teaching for a stroke caregiver was truly effective?

options.A: Handing the family a large textbook on neurology on the day of discharge
options.B: Telling the family to call emergency services for any routine question
options.C: Assuming family members already know how to operate transfer belts
options.D: Teaching care techniques in small, manageable steps with return demonstrations

explanation: Having them show you back (return demonstration) is the best way to make sure they feel confident and safe doing it at home.

question: In traditional Nigerian society, who has mainly taken care of older adults needing support?

options.A: Government-run hospitals
options.B: Non-profit religious charities
options.C: Extended family networks
options.D: Private nursing homes

explanation: You got this! Culturally, our extended family system has always been the primary safety net for caring for our aging loved ones.

question: Why are formal nursing homes slowly becoming more common in modern Nigeria?

options.A: Elderly individuals prefer living away from relatives
options.B: Traditional family values have completely disappeared
options.C: Urban migration and changing economic structures
options.D: A government ban on caring for elders at home

explanation: Spot on! As younger family members move to busy cities for work and economic pressures rise, traditional home care setups have become harder to maintain.

question: What is the main goal of nursing care in a long-term care facility, compared to a busy acute hospital?

options.A: Maintaining quality of life and preserving function
options.B: Performing high-risk surgical procedures daily
options.C: Treating acute infectious disease outbreaks only
options.D: Rapid stabilization and immediate discharge

explanation: Exactly! Unlike emergency wards meant for quick discharges, long-term homes focus on daily comfort, happiness, and keeping residents as independent as possible.

question: You notice a care assistant rushing an elderly resident through a meal. What should you do first as the nurse?

options.A: Educate the assistant on patient-centered feeding techniques and safety
options.B: Report the assistant to the police for physical abuse immediately
options.C: Ignore the incident since assistants are trained separately
options.D: Take over feeding all residents in the facility personally

explanation: Well done! As a nurse, you supervise support staff. Teaching them the right, gentle way to feed residents ensures safe and dignified care.

question: Why do nurses perform a full assessment when a new resident is admitted to a care facility?

options.A: To establish a baseline and identify individual health risks
options.B: To diagnose new acute infectious diseases
options.C: To determine the exact date the resident will be discharged
options.D: To fulfill a legal requirement without affecting care

explanation: Great job! This initial check helps you know what is 'normal' for the resident so you can easily spot things like fall risks early on.

question: Why must a resident's care plan be updated regularly?

options.A: Hospital regulations require paperwork changes every week
options.B: Resident health status and functional abilities change
options.C: Family members demand a new format monthly
options.D: Staff members prefer writing new plans frequently

explanation: Spot on! People change over time. Care plans must grow and adapt to match the resident's current physical or medical condition.

question: Why should nurses encourage elderly residents to do parts of their own bath and hygiene care?

options.A: To preserve their dignity and functional independence
options.B: To lower the financial cost of facility operations
options.C: To eliminate the need for any assistive devices
options.D: To reduce the workload of the nursing staff completely

explanation: You got it! Doing things for themselves—even small tasks—helps residents keep their strength and feel good about their independence.

question: A care assistant is about to feed a resident who has trouble swallowing. What safety tip should you give?

options.A: Offer large chunks of solid food for better chewing
options.B: Feed the resident as quickly as possible
options.C: Position the resident in an upright sitting posture
options.D: Encourage the resident to lie flat on the bed

explanation: Brilliant! Sitting upright uses gravity to help swallowing and keeps food out of the lungs, preventing dangerous choking.

question: What is the medical term for when a patient takes many different medications at the same time?

options.A: Adverse reaction
options.B: Therapeutic synergy
options.C: Polypharmacy
options.D: Pharmacokinetics

explanation: Correct! 'Poly' means many, and 'pharmacy' means drugs. Polypharmacy simply means managing multiple medications at once.

question: Why are older adults more likely to experience drug toxicity than younger adults?

options.A: Age-related decline in kidney and liver function
options.B: Older cells are completely immune to drugs
options.C: Their bodies absorb all medications instantly
options.D: They always take higher doses than prescribed

explanation: Spot on! Because the kidneys and liver process and clear drugs more slowly as we age, medications stay active longer, increasing the risk of buildup.

question: What is a key nursing action to prevent bedsores (pressure injuries) in a resident who stays in bed all day?

options.A: Applying dry heat directly to bony prominences
options.B: Implementing regular repositioning schedules
options.C: Encouraging complete bed rest at all times
options.D: Restricting fluid intake to keep skin dry

explanation: You got it! Turning or shifting the resident regularly takes the weight off vulnerable skin, keeping the blood flowing nicely.

question: How should a nurse respectfully address an older adult resident in Nigeria?

options.A: Using numbers assigned to their room beds
options.B: Using respectful honorific titles and polite language
options.C: By their first name to encourage casual friendliness
options.D: By referring to their specific medical diagnosis

explanation: Exactly! In our culture, showing respect to elders through proper titles like 'Mama', 'Papa', or respectful greetings goes a long way.

question: What should you do if an older resident has severe memory loss and cannot give informed consent for a procedure?

options.A: Ask other residents in the facility to decide
options.B: Discontinue all nursing care until memory returns
options.C: Proceed with all care without discussing it with anyone
options.D: Consult the designated family surrogate decision-maker

explanation: Spot on! When a resident can no longer make decisions for themselves, we involve their legally appointed family spokesperson to guide their care.

question: What is the main goal of a rehabilitation hospital?

options.A: Restoring lost function and maximizing independence
options.B: Treating acute infectious disease outbreaks
options.C: Stabilizing immediate life-threatening organ failure
options.D: Providing long-term terminal palliative care

explanation: You got this! Rehab hospitals help patients rebuild their strength and everyday skills after major life changes, rather than managing sudden medical emergencies.

question: How does a rehab facility differ from a regular acute care hospital ward?

options.A: Rehab facilities deal strictly with infectious diseases, while acute care wards handle surgeries.
options.B: Rehab facilities prohibit family visitation to protect the therapy schedule.
options.C: Acute care hospitals do not employ registered nurses, whereas rehab facilities are nurse-run.
options.D: Acute care focuses on life-saving stabilization, while rehab focuses on restoring functional independence.

explanation: Spot on! Acute care handles the active crisis, while rehab steps in once the patient is stable enough to focus on long-term recovery and therapy.

question: Which major complication do rehabilitation nurses constantly work to prevent?

options.A: Sudden visual impairment
options.B: Spontaneous bone fractures
options.C: Acute myocardial infarction
options.D: Pressure injuries and contractures

explanation: Great job! Because rehab patients often spend a lot of time resting, nurses watch closely to prevent bed sores (pressure injuries) and stiff joints (contractures).

question: Why should patients always be involved in setting their own rehabilitation goals?

options.A: It ensures the recovery targets matter to the patient's actual daily life.
options.B: It completely removes the need for physical therapy oversight.
options.C: Hospital accreditation rules legally prohibit nurse-only care plans.
options.D: Patients have medical degrees that guide clinical interventions.

explanation: Exactly! When patients help choose what they want to achieve, they feel more motivated to push through tough therapy sessions.

question: Which member of the healthcare team helps a patient relearn how to swallow safely?

options.A: Clinical Pharmacist
options.B: Physical Therapist
options.C: Speech-Language Pathologist
options.D: Occupational Therapist

explanation: Well done! Speech-Language Pathologists do much more than speech—they are experts in evaluating and treating swallowing difficulties too.

question: A stroke patient is struggling to button their shirt and brush their teeth. Which specialist should the nurse call first?

options.A: Occupational Therapist
options.B: Physical Therapist
options.C: Respiratory Therapist
options.D: Dietitian

explanation: Spot on! Occupational therapists focus on upper body strength and everyday activities like dressing, bathing, and grooming.

question: What is the main reason nurses use functional assessment tools in a rehab ward?

options.A: To calculate the exact date of hospital discharge
options.B: To measure how much assistance a patient needs with daily activities
options.C: To determine daily caloric requirements
options.D: To diagnose underlying genetic mutations

explanation: You got it! These tools help us clearly see how independent a patient is and track their progress over time.

question: Why is an individualized care plan so important in rehabilitation?

options.A: It prevents nurses from having to document patient progress.
options.B: Patients with the same medical diagnosis can have completely different functional abilities and personal goals.
options.C: Insurance companies refuse to pay for care plans that mention physical therapy.
options.D: Standardized care plans are illegal in specialized hospital settings.

explanation: Exactly! No two patients are alike, even with the same diagnosis. Their care must fit their unique lifestyle, support system, and personal goals.

question: What is the main benefit of using hydrotherapy (water exercise) in rehab?

options.A: Water buoyancy reduces joint stress during physical exercise.
options.B: It replaces the need for any nutritional support.
options.C: It eliminates all risks of secondary skin infections.
options.D: It completely cures chronic neurological disorders in days.

explanation: Well done! The water helps support the patient's weight, taking pressure off painful or weak joints so they can move more easily.

question: Why is electrical muscle stimulation sometimes used during physical rehabilitation?

options.A: To permanently replace voluntary muscle contraction
options.B: To help re-educate and stimulate muscles that have lost nerve signaling
options.C: To provide general systemic pain relief like a warm bath
options.D: To rapidly increase red blood cell production

explanation: Spot on! Gentle electrical pulses can help wake up and contract muscles that aren't receiving normal signals from the brain yet.

question: Why is 'activity pacing' so important when working with chronic patients in rehab?

options.A: Pacing ensures that nurses do not have to assist with patient transfers.
options.B: Hospital policies state that therapy cannot exceed twenty minutes per day.
options.C: Pushing patients past their physical limits can cause exhaustion and hinder overall recovery.
options.D: Chronic conditions make patients completely immune to physical fatigue.

explanation: You got it! Balancing therapy with enough rest prevents burnout and keeps the patient energized for their recovery journey.

question: A patient with heart failure and a leg amputation suddenly gets short of breath and has swollen ankles during therapy. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Immediate complete recovery of cardiac function
options.B: Signs of fluid overload requiring immediate evaluation
options.C: An expected side effect of occupational therapy
options.D: Normal muscle growth from the therapy session

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Sudden swelling and shortness of breath in a heart failure patient are classic red flags for fluid overload that need quick assessment.

question: When should discharge planning ideally begin in a rehabilitation hospital?

options.A: Only after the final therapy session is completed
options.B: Twenty-four hours before the patient leaves
options.C: When the insurance company stops paying for care
options.D: The moment the patient is admitted to the facility

explanation: Spot on! Starting discharge planning early ensures that home equipment, family training, and support services are ready without a last-minute rush.

question: Why is caregiver training a crucial part of the discharge process in rehab?

options.A: It replaces the need for home health nursing visits.
options.B: It allows the hospital to discharge nursing staff members.
options.C: It ensures family members can safely assist with daily transfers and care at home.
options.D: It legally transfers hospital liability entirely to the family members.

explanation: Well done! Families need hands-on practice in a safe setting so they can care for their loved one at home without hurting themselves or the patient.

question: Which safety incident is most frequently tracked in rehabilitation hospital quality reports?

options.A: Newborn abductions
options.B: Patient falls
options.C: Surgical site fires
options.D: Radiation overexposure

explanation: You got it! Because rehab patients are actively learning how to move and walk again, preventing and tracking falls is a top priority.

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting quality improvement reviews in a rehab facility?

options.A: To identify safety risks and find ways to improve patient care outcomes
options.B: To increase the cost of hospital admission fees
options.C: To find individual staff members to punish for making mistakes
options.D: To reduce the number of therapy hours required by insurance

explanation: Spot on! Quality improvement is all about making systems safer and patient care better—it's never about assigning blame.

question: What is the main purpose of a skilled nursing facility (SNF)?

options.A: To replace standard emergency room hospital services
options.B: To act as a daycare center for healthy older adults
options.C: To offer permanent housing without medical supervision
options.D: To provide 24-hour medical care and rehabilitation

explanation: Think of a skilled nursing facility as a place for round-the-clock care and therapy when patients are recovering or need ongoing clinical support. You've got this!

question: When do patients most commonly move into a skilled nursing facility?

options.A: When they want to change their primary care physician
options.B: Immediately following a hospital stay for acute illness or surgery
options.C: Right after receiving a routine annual checkup from a family doctor
options.D: Before an elective outpatient procedure scheduled next month

explanation: Most patients step down from the hospital to an SNF when they still need professional nursing care before heading back home. Great clinical insight!

question: Which healthcare professional helps residents recover their ability to do everyday tasks like dressing and bathing?

options.A: Pharmacy delivery
options.B: Occupational therapy
options.C: Wound debridement
options.D: Intravenous therapy

explanation: Occupational therapy helps patients regain everyday self-care skills so they can live as independently as possible. Keep up the great work!

question: A resident needs daily sterile dressing changes for a deep surgical wound. Which facility type is best suited for this care?

options.A: An adult day care center
options.B: A skilled nursing facility
options.C: A standard retirement community
options.D: An independent living apartment

explanation: Complex sterile wound care requires the expert clinical hands and continuous monitoring found in a skilled nursing facility. Spot on!

question: What is typically required by health insurance or Medicare to cover a stay in a skilled nursing facility?

options.A: A mandatory surgical procedure of any kind
options.B: Proof of full private health insurance coverage
options.C: A written referral from a public health minister
options.D: A qualifying hospital stay of at least three days

explanation: Insurance rules usually require at least three consecutive inpatient hospital days before they will help cover skilled nursing care.

question: A patient wants to enter an SNF simply because they feel lonely at home and need help cooking meals. Why might this admission be delayed or denied coverage?

options.A: Social workers are not allowed to review home situations
options.B: The patient lacks a need for daily skilled nursing or therapy services
options.C: Medicare covers custodial care for anyone requesting it
options.D: The facility only accepts patients with infectious diseases

explanation: SNF coverage is meant for active medical or therapy needs, rather than basic social support or housekeeping help. Makes total sense!

question: Who is usually the first member of the nursing team to notice small, daily changes in a resident's condition?

options.A: Director of nursing
options.B: Billing administrator
options.C: Facility pharmacist
options.D: Certified nursing assistant

explanation: Certified nursing assistants (CNAs) spend the most time with residents, making them amazing at spotting early signs of a change in health!

question: Why is regular communication between nursing assistants and registered nurses so important in an SNF?

options.A: Registered nurses need assistants to write formal medical diagnoses
options.B: Registered nurses only work during night shifts
options.C: Nursing assistants report early warning signs like skin breakdown to the RN
options.D: Nursing assistants are legally required to manage all IV therapy

explanation: Teamwork is key! When assistants share what they see, the RN can step in early before a small issue becomes a big problem.

question: Which team member takes the lead in evaluating a resident's nutrition and managing special diets?

options.A: Registered dietitian
options.B: Social worker
options.C: Physical therapist
options.D: Activities director

explanation: Registered dietitians assess nutrition needs, track weight changes, and design healthy meal plans tailored to each resident.
