question: What is the main benefit of regular team meetings among different healthcare professionals in an SNF?

options.A: To coordinate diverse professional insights and prevent conflicting care plans
options.B: To reduce the number of visitors allowed in the facility
options.C: To allow administrators to review employee attendance records
options.D: To replace the need for daily nursing assessments and vital sign checks

explanation: When nursing, therapy, and kitchen staff meet together, everyone works toward the exact same patient goals. Teamwork makes the dream work!

question: What is the main purpose of the Minimum Data Set (MDS) assessment tool in a skilled nursing facility?

options.A: To calculate monthly billing statements for the facility kitchen
options.B: To schedule daily transportation for outpatient doctor visits
options.C: To replace physician progress notes in the main chart
options.D: To serve as a standardized assessment tool driving the care plan

explanation: The MDS is a comprehensive evaluation tool that helps nurses track a resident's health and guide their personalized care plan.

question: A nurse notices a resident's memory and thinking have suddenly gotten worse over two days. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Wait until the next scheduled quarterly MDS review to mention the change
options.B: Perform a focused assessment and document the changes clearly in the clinical record
options.C: Remove the resident from the care plan entirely
options.D: Update the facility menu without notifying the medical provider

explanation: Sudden health changes always require quick evaluation and clear, accurate charting so doctors can step in right away.

question: What is the main goal of restorative nursing care in an SNF?

options.A: To reinforce therapy goals during everyday routine activities
options.B: To administer complex intravenous medications overnight
options.C: To replace formal physical therapy sessions entirely
options.D: To manage facility financial records and insurance claims

explanation: Restorative nursing helps residents practice their therapy skills during daily routines so they can hold onto their independence.

question: Why are gentle range-of-motion exercises and turning schedules crucial for residents who cannot move much on their own?

options.A: To speed up the metabolic rate and cure underlying chronic infections
options.B: To prevent secondary complications like contractures and pressure injuries
options.C: To eliminate the need for any nutritional support or dietary supplements
options.D: To guarantee that the resident will never need assistance walking again

explanation: Moving and turning patients keeps their joints flexible and protects their skin from painful pressure sores. Excellent nursing practice!

question: Which agency sets and enforces the main federal regulations for skilled nursing facilities?

options.A: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
options.B: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)
options.C: World Health Organization (WHO)
options.D: National Institutes of Health (NIH)

explanation: CMS oversees the federal rules and quality standards that certified skilled nursing facilities must follow. You're building a strong regulatory foundation!

question: Which of the following is NOT a focus area during a health inspection survey in an SNF?

options.A: Infection control practices and hand hygiene compliance
options.B: Medication administration safety and storage
options.C: Stock market investments of the facility parent corporation
options.D: Resident rights and protection from abuse or neglect

explanation: Health inspectors look at patient safety, care quality, and resident rights—not corporate financial portfolios!

question: When should discharge planning ideally begin for a resident admitted to an SNF?

options.A: After Medicare coverage expires
options.B: On the day of admission
options.C: When the family requests it
options.D: Forty-eight hours before leaving

explanation: Starting discharge planning right away ensures home support and equipment are ready well before the patient leaves. Smart nursing starts early!

question: What is the biggest risk of a poorly planned transition when a resident leaves the SNF to go back home?

options.A: An avoidable hospital readmission due to lack of preparation
options.B: Immediate disciplinary action against the resident by Medicare
options.C: A mandatory extension of the SNF stay for two full years
options.D: The automatic cancellation of all future doctor appointments

explanation: Without clear medication guides and home help, discharged patients often suffer setbacks that send them right back to the hospital.

question: What is the main purpose of a care home?

options.A: Providing accommodation and support for people who cannot live alone
options.B: Acting as a temporary shelter for travelers and homeless individuals
options.C: Providing short-term rehabilitation solely for orthopedic injuries
options.D: Serving exclusively as a long-term hospital ward for acute surgical cases

explanation: You got this! Care homes are wonderful places designed to house and support individuals who need ongoing daily assistance due to age or chronic health needs.

question: How do residential care homes differ basically from nursing homes?

options.A: Nursing homes feature 24-hour medical staff for complex health needs, while residential care focuses on daily living assistance
options.B: Residential care homes are operated by the government, while nursing homes are private
options.C: Residential care homes are exclusively for children, whereas nursing homes are strictly for the elderly
options.D: Nursing homes do not provide meals, unlike standard residential care facilities

explanation: Spot on! The big difference is clinical staffing: nursing homes have 24-hour medical care for heavy health needs, while residential homes focus more on daily living support.

question: Which type of care home offers short-term stays to give family caregivers a quick break?

options.A: Nursing care
options.B: Respite care
options.C: Dementia care
options.D: Palliative care

explanation: Brilliant! Respite care gives family members a much-needed temporary break by stepping in to handle care duties for a short while.

question: Why do dementia units usually have secure, controlled exits?

options.A: To comply with federal fire safety codes for chemical storage rooms
options.B: To punish residents who refuse to participate in daily group activities
options.C: To restrict family members from visiting outside of strict morning hours
options.D: To prevent wandering and keep residents with memory loss safe

explanation: Correct! Wandering is very common in advanced dementia, so secure doors keep our vulnerable residents safe from getting lost.

question: Why must care homes undergo regular government inspections?

options.A: To determine the weekly menu options for the dining hall
options.B: To collect annual property taxes directly from the facility owners
options.C: To ensure compliance with safety, sanitation, and quality standards
options.D: To recruit nursing students for government hospital positions

explanation: You nailed it! Regular checks make sure facilities keep up high standards of cleanliness, safety, and patient care.

question: Which of these is NOT checked during a care home regulatory inspection?

options.A: Sanitation and food hygiene practices in the kitchen
options.B: Proper storage and administration of resident medications
options.C: Staff-to-resident ratios on every shift
options.D: Personal investment portfolios of the facility directors

explanation: Well done! Inspectors focus entirely on resident safety, health, and facility standards—not the private finances of management.

question: What is the main reason a nurse uses the Braden Scale when a resident is admitted?

options.A: Measuring the severity of cognitive memory loss
options.B: Determining the level of financial independence
options.C: Evaluating the daily nutritional caloric intake
options.D: Assessing the risk of developing pressure injuries

explanation: Awesome! The Braden Scale is a fantastic, standard nursing tool used to predict and prevent skin breakdown.

question: A newly admitted resident is very quiet and refuses to interact with others. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Immediately discharge the resident back home for family care
options.B: Prescribe a mild sedative medication to calm their anxiety
options.C: Ignore the behavior since adjustment to a new home takes weeks
options.D: Conduct a comprehensive holistic assessment including psychological and social history

explanation: Spot on! Before jumping to conclusions, a warm, thorough assessment helps us find out if they are dealing with depression or fear so we can support them properly.

question: What is the main focus of person-centred care in a care home?

options.A: Focusing solely on the medical diagnosis rather than the person
options.B: Reducing operational expenses by standardizing daily meal schedules
options.C: Enforcing strict institutional routines for the convenience of the nursing staff
options.D: Tailoring care around the individual resident's unique preferences and life history

explanation: You got it! Person-centred care means treating the resident as a unique individual with their own habits, likes, and life story.

question: Why do nurses encourage residents to do parts of their daily care on their own?

options.A: To test whether the resident is trying to escape from the facility
options.B: To comply with legal mandates that forbid nurses from assisting with bathing
options.C: To preserve resident dignity, maintain functional ability, and promote autonomy
options.D: To reduce the number of staff members needed on duty during night shifts

explanation: Brilliant! Encouraging self-care helps older adults stay active, independent, and proud of what they can still do.

question: What is polypharmacy, a common concern in care home residents?

options.A: The legal distribution of herbal remedies without a doctor's order
options.B: The allergic reaction caused by taking antibiotics with food
options.C: The practice of storing drugs in a centralized facility pharmacy
options.D: The concurrent use of multiple medications by a single patient

explanation: Correct! Polypharmacy simply means taking many different drugs at the same time, which requires careful monitoring by nurses to avoid bad reactions.

question: How should controlled substances be stored in a residential care home?

options.A: In a secure double-lock system with strict inventory logs
options.B: In the kitchen refrigerator alongside resident food supplies
options.C: In an open cabinet in the nurses' station for quick access
options.D: Inside the resident's personal bedside drawer for self-administration

explanation: Well done! Because controlled drugs carry a high risk of misuse, they must always be double-locked and carefully tracked.

question: Which professional helps residents adapt their living spaces to prevent falls and keep moving safely?

options.A: Hospital billing accountant
options.B: Facility maintenance engineer
options.C: Occupational or physiotherapist
options.D: Clinical research pharmacist

explanation: Spot on! Therapists are experts at checking physical ability and recommending exercises or environmental changes to stop falls.

question: Why are regular multidisciplinary team meetings so important in a care home?

options.A: To allow different healthcare professionals to coordinate care and review resident progress
options.B: To give the facility director a chance to discipline underperforming employees
options.C: To discuss financial profits and budgeting with resident families
options.D: To replace the need for individual nursing care plans altogether

explanation: You nailed it! When nursing, medical, and therapy staff talk regularly, everyone works together as a unified team for the resident.

question: What is the main focus of palliative care in a residential care home?

options.A: Discharging residents to an acute hospital ward immediately
options.B: Aggressive medical interventions to cure terminal chronic illnesses
options.C: Providing comfort, pain management, and dignity during end-of-life
options.D: Restricting family visits to maintain strict facility quiet hours

explanation: Brilliant! Palliative care is all about comforting patients, easing pain, and giving them dignity when curing is no longer possible.

question: What is the purpose of an advance care directive in nursing practice?

options.A: To state a resident's medical treatment preferences before they lose decision-making capacity
options.B: To outline the daily cleaning schedule for the resident's private room
options.C: To mandate immediate emergency surgery for all sudden health crises
options.D: To authorize the nursing staff to make financial investments on behalf of the family

explanation: Correct! An advance directive lets patients clearly state what medical treatments they want or do not want before they become unable to decide.

question: What is the main purpose of a geriatric home?

options.A: Providing daycare services exclusively for working parents
options.B: Offering temporary quarantine for infectious diseases
options.C: Serving as a permanent substitute for acute surgical hospitals
options.D: Providing specialized residential care for older adults

explanation: Geriatric homes are set up to look after older adults who need a bit of help with their daily activities. You've got this!

question: Why has the demand for formal geriatric homes been on the rise lately?

options.A: Urbanization and changing family structures
options.B: Older adults universally preferring institutional living
options.C: Government bans on caring for elderly relatives at home
options.D: The complete disappearance of traditional family values

explanation: As cities grow and more family members move away for work, formal residential care becomes necessary to support our elders. Great job thinking it through!

question: How does the nurse-patient relationship in a geriatric home usually differ from an acute care hospital?

options.A: It requires no communication with family members
options.B: It focuses exclusively on surgical recovery
options.C: It involves only one-time emergency interventions
options.D: It is typically long-term and relationship-focused

explanation: Because care lasts months or years, nurses get to build warm, lasting relationships with the residents. It is one of the most rewarding parts of nursing!

question: Which of these is a key advocacy role for a nurse working in a geriatric home?

options.A: Enforcing strict institutional routines without exception
options.B: Ensuring residents retain their dignity and rights
options.C: Making all financial decisions for the resident
options.D: Replacing family members during social visits

explanation: Nurses stand up for older adults to make sure their personal choices and human rights are always respected. You are their voice!

question: What does a Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment primarily look at?

options.A: Occupational history and retirement savings
options.B: Physical, functional, psychological, and social well-being
options.C: Surgical fitness for emergency organ transplants
options.D: Childhood developmental milestones

explanation: A Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment looks at the whole person—not just physical symptoms, but how they function, their mood, and their social life too.

question: A resident suddenly becomes confused and restless. What should you suspect first instead of brushing it off as normal aging?

options.A: A deliberate attempt to gain attention from staff
options.B: A permanent personality change due to boredom
options.C: A normal and expected part of getting older
options.D: An acute problem like delirium caused by an infection

explanation: Sudden confusion is never just 'old age.' It is often a red flag that something acute is going on, like a urinary tract infection or dehydration. Good clinical thinking!

question: Which types of medications most commonly increase the risk of falls in older adults?

options.A: Multivitamins
options.B: Topical antifungal creams
options.C: Sedatives and antihypertensives
options.D: Vitamin C supplements

explanation: Drugs that cause dizziness, sleepiness, or sudden drops in blood pressure can easily lead to a fall. Always keep an eye on safety!

question: A resident says they feel unsteady walking to the dining hall. What is your best first nursing action?

options.A: Assess their footwear, use of assistive devices, and recent medications
options.B: Scold the resident for walking without supervision
options.C: Restrict all fluid intake to prevent bathroom trips
options.D: Advise the resident to stay permanently in bed for safety

explanation: Finding the exact cause—like bad shoes, a missing walking stick, or a dizzying drug side effect—helps fix the problem at the root. Spot on!

question: What do we mean by the term 'polypharmacy'?

options.A: Taking only herbal remedies
options.B: The concurrent use of multiple medications
options.C: The total rejection of all prescribed drugs
options.D: An allergy to multiple antibiotics

explanation: Polypharmacy simply means taking several different drugs at the same time, which happens often when managing multiple chronic illnesses in older age.

question: Why are older adults more likely to experience adverse drug reactions?

options.A: Their bodies absorb medications much faster than younger people
options.B: Older skin cannot absorb pills properly
options.C: They always refuse to take prescribed doses
options.D: Age-related slowdown in kidney and liver function

explanation: As we age, our kidneys and liver process drugs more slowly. This means medications stay in the body longer and can build up to toxic levels.

question: Why are older adults at a much higher risk for dehydration?

options.A: Their bodies require zero water intake after age sixty
options.B: They sweat significantly more than younger adults
options.C: Fluid absorption is blocked completely in the stomach
options.D: They have a blunted thirst response and may not feel thirsty

explanation: The natural body mechanism that tells us we are thirsty slows down with age, so older adults often won't drink unless we gently remind and encourage them.

question: What is a major nursing concern when an older adult has severe dental problems and missing teeth?

options.A: Increased likelihood of developing hypertension
options.B: Rapid cognitive decline within forty-eight hours
options.C: Immediate kidney failure due to poor digestion
options.D: Risk of malnutrition and difficulty chewing certain foods

explanation: When chewing hurts or is difficult, residents might skip healthy foods like meat and raw veggies unless their meals are specially prepared. You are learning great clinical foresight!

question: What is the primary goal of palliative care in a geriatric setting?

options.A: Finding a complete cure for terminal chronic illnesses
options.B: Improving quality of life and managing comfort and symptoms
options.C: Eliminating the need for family visits during illness
options.D: Speeding up the dying process to save facility resources

explanation: Palliative care focuses entirely on comfort, dignity, and easing pain so the resident can live their final days with peace. Beautiful nursing concept!

question: Why is advance care planning so important for older adults?

options.A: It guarantees that residents will never experience physical pain
options.B: It ensures the resident's personal wishes for end-of-life care are known and honored
options.C: It prevents nurses from having to communicate with grieving relatives
options.D: It legally forces family members to pay for expensive surgeries

explanation: Talking about preferences early on ensures that future medical decisions truly reflect what the resident wants when they can no longer speak for themselves.

question: Which of these is NOT an ethical responsibility of a nurse in a geriatric home?

options.A: Maintaining strict medical confidentiality
options.B: Ignoring resident complaints to save time
options.C: Protecting vulnerable adults from abuse
options.D: Respecting the personal autonomy of the resident

explanation: Ignoring a resident's complaints breaks professional ethics and patient trust. A great nurse always listens and takes action!

question: Why do geriatric facilities regularly conduct quality improvement audits?

options.A: To increase the cost of care for incoming residents
options.B: To eliminate the need for any government oversight
options.C: To ensure care practices remain safe, compassionate, and evidence-based
options.D: To find reasons to dismiss hardworking nursing staff

explanation: Audits help catch gaps in care early, prevent mistakes, and keep the environment safe and comforting for every resident. You're doing brilliantly!

question: What is the primary focus of a hospice home facility?

options.A: Delivering intensive acute surgical care
options.B: Testing experimental medical treatments
options.C: Providing comfort and quality of life
options.D: Achieving a full recovery from terminal illness

explanation: Hospice care shifts away from curative treatments and focuses entirely on keeping the patient comfortable and improving their quality of life. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h1)

question: Why are hospice homes designed to feel homelike rather than clinical?

options.A: To reduce the anxiety associated with traditional hospitals
options.B: To encourage patients to continue active physical therapy
options.C: To make it easier for doctors to perform major surgeries
options.D: To lower operational costs for the healthcare facility

explanation: A familiar, comfortable environment helps ease the psychological stress and fear that patients often feel in sterile hospital wards. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h1)

question: How does hospice philosophy view the dying process?

options.A: As an unpredictable event requiring intensive surgery
options.B: As a natural part of the human life cycle
options.C: As a condition that can always be reversed with therapy
options.D: As a medical failure that must be fought at all costs

explanation: Hospice care embraces dying as a normal stage of life rather than viewing it purely as a medical failure. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h2)

question: What is the main goal of respecting patient autonomy in end-of-life care?

options.A: Reducing the workload of the attending nursing staff
options.B: Ensuring family members make all major medical decisions
options.C: Allowing the patient to keep control over their choices
options.D: Speeding up the discharge process from the facility

explanation: Respecting autonomy means empowering the patient to direct their own care and make meaningful decisions about their remaining time. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h2)

question: What is the standard estimated life expectancy required for hospice admission?

options.A: Two years or less
options.B: One year or less
options.C: One month or less
options.D: Six months or less

explanation: Standard admission guidelines require a physician certification that the patient's life expectancy is six months or less. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h3)

question: A patient is admitted to a hospice facility. What must they or their surrogate agree to regarding their treatment?

options.A: To participate in experimental clinical drug trials
options.B: To undergo aggressive physical rehabilitation daily
options.C: To stop curative treatments and focus on comfort
options.D: To transfer back to an acute care hospital weekly

explanation: Choosing hospice care means electing to forego curative therapies in favor of comfort-focused palliative management. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h3)

question: Which member of the hospice team primarily helps families navigate financial and social resource planning?

options.A: The medical social worker
options.B: The hospice facility chaplain
options.C: The attending medical physician
options.D: The certified nursing assistant

explanation: Social workers are trained to help families manage financial concerns, legal documents, and community support resources. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h4)

question: A family caregiver is exhausted and needs a short break to run errands. Which hospice team member is best suited to sit with the patient during this time?

options.A: A medical social worker
options.B: A registered nurse
options.C: A hospice volunteer
options.D: A certified nursing assistant

explanation: Volunteers frequently provide companionship and respite care, giving family caregivers time away to rest or attend to personal errands. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h4)

question: Why are pain medications often given on a scheduled, around-the-clock basis in hospice care?

options.A: To prevent severe breakthrough pain before it starts
options.B: To eliminate the need for any nursing pain assessments
options.C: To help the patient regain full physical strength
options.D: To ensure the patient stays unconscious all day

explanation: Scheduled dosing maintains steady blood levels of pain medication, preventing pain from escalating into severe episodes. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h5)

question: A patient with terminal cancer is unable to speak but is frowning, restless, and breathing rapidly. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: The patient is fully relaxed and ready for sleep
options.B: The patient is recovering normal neurological function
options.C: The patient is having an allergic reaction to food
options.D: The patient is experiencing untreated pain or discomfort

explanation: Non-verbal patients often show pain and distress through behavioral cues like frowning, restlessness, and changes in respiratory rate. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h5)

question: What is the most appropriate nursing response when a dying patient expresses deep existential fear?

options.A: Telling the patient not to worry because everything is fine
options.B: Changing the subject immediately to a cheerful topic
options.C: Listening actively and validating their emotional feelings
options.D: Insisting that the patient talk to a psychiatrist today

explanation: Patients benefit most when nurses listen patiently and acknowledge their fears without dismissing them or offering false comfort. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical goal of psychosocial support in hospice care?

options.A: Providing a safe space for emotional expression
options.B: Honoring the patient's personal faith and spiritual traditions
options.C: Helping the patient resolve all past family conflicts instantly
options.D: Supporting family members through anticipatory grief

explanation: While nurses support emotional processing, resolving lifelong family conflicts is rarely guaranteed or realistic in a short time frame. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h6)

question: What legal document outlines a patient's specific wishes regarding life-sustaining medical treatments?

options.A: A hospital discharge summary sheet
options.B: A physician prescription log
options.C: An advance directive or living will
options.D: A standard health insurance claim form

explanation: Living wills and advance directives legally document a person's preferences for medical interventions when they can no longer speak for themselves. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h7)

question: Why is cultural competence essential when caring for patients at the end of life?

options.A: It allows the nurse to bypass signing advance directives
options.B: It legally forces family members to accept Western medicine
options.C: Death practices and mourning rituals vary widely across cultures
options.D: It eliminates all emotional distress for the family

explanation: Understanding cultural differences ensures that nurses respect family traditions surrounding dying, pain management, and grief. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h7)

question: When does bereavement support typically begin and end in a hospice program?

options.A: It begins only after one full year has passed
options.B: It continues for months after the patient passes away
options.C: It only occurs during the final week of the patient's life
options.D: It stops immediately the moment the patient dies

explanation: Bereavement care is an ongoing service that supports grieving family members for many months following their loss. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h8)

question: What is a primary purpose of follow-up bereavement services provided by a hospice team?

options.A: To help surviving family members navigate their grief
options.B: To collect remaining financial payments for the facility
options.C: To conduct research on terminal disease progression
options.D: To evaluate the medical skills of the nursing staff

explanation: Support groups and counseling help families cope with the emotional and physical challenges of the grieving process. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T14#GNS324_U5_T14_h8)

question: What is the main focus of a maternity home in the community?

options.A: Managing low-risk pregnancies and normal deliveries
options.B: Treating chronic illnesses in elderly patients
options.C: Performing major complex obstetric surgeries
options.D: Providing long-term pediatric intensive care

explanation: You've got this! Maternity homes are set up to handle normal, healthy pregnancies and deliveries right in the neighborhood.

question: Why are maternity homes so important in rural Nigerian communities?

options.A: They replace federal tertiary teaching hospitals completely
options.B: They eliminate the need for any medications during labor
options.C: They offer free surgical care funded by international donors
options.D: They serve as local bridges to care when distant hospitals are hard to reach

explanation: Spot on! By being close by, they bridge the gap so mums don't have to travel huge distances just to get basic care.

question: Which body regulates nursing and midwifery practice in Nigeria?

options.A: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria
options.B: Pharmacists Council of National Health
options.C: Medical and Dental Consultants Association
options.D: National Union of Allied Health Workers

explanation: That's right! The NMCN sets the standards for our training and practice across the country.

question: What is the main reason regulatory bodies inspect private maternity homes?

options.A: To dictate the daily menu options for admitted patients
options.B: To ensure compliance with safety standards and prevent quackery
options.C: To collect taxes on behalf of international health groups
options.D: To supply free prescription medications to the facility

explanation: Well done! Routine checks make sure facilities keep things clean, safe, and professional to protect mums and babies.

question: What routine test is done on a pregnant woman's urine during antenatal visits?

options.A: Thyroid hormone titers
options.B: Serum electrolyte balance
options.C: Liver enzyme concentrations
options.D: Protein and glucose levels

explanation: Correct! Checking urine helps us catch protein (a sign of pre-eclampsia) or glucose (a sign of gestational diabetes) early.

question: A mum at 28 weeks comes in with a BP of 140/90 mmHg and swollen ankles. What should you do next?

options.A: Perform further evaluation and prepare for possible referral
options.B: Reassure her that swelling is completely normal at all times
options.C: Administer heavy routine sedatives immediately
options.D: Discharge her home with instructions to rest for a week

explanation: You nailed it! High BP and swelling late in pregnancy are red flags for pre-eclampsia that need close checking and quick action.

question: What is the main use of a partograph during active labor?

options.A: To record the financial bills accrued by the patient
options.B: To track the progress of labor and spot deviations early
options.C: To schedule the exact minute the baby will be born
options.D: To calculate the exact birth weight of the baby beforehand

explanation: Spot on! The partograph gives a clear picture of how labor is going, helping us catch any trouble early.

question: Why do we encourage skin-to-skin contact right after a normal delivery?

options.A: It completely prevents the mother from experiencing postpartum bleeding
options.B: It speeds up the surgical healing of an episiotomy wound
options.C: It acts as a permanent immunization against childhood illnesses
options.D: It helps regulate the newborn's body temperature and encourages breastfeeding

explanation: That's right! Mum's body heat keeps the baby warm, and it gets breastfeeding off to a great start.

question: Which injection is routinely given to newborns to prevent bleeding?

options.A: Calcium gluconate
options.B: Magnesium sulfate
options.C: Vitamin K
options.D: Vitamin C

explanation: Great job! Babies are born with low vitamin K levels, so this shot protects them from bleeding problems.

question: Why do midwives frequently check if the uterus is firm after delivery?

options.A: To test the mother's abdominal muscle strength after labor
options.B: To ensure the uterine muscle is contracting well to prevent hemorrhage
options.C: To measure the exact amount of amniotic fluid left inside
options.D: To check if the baby is positioned correctly for feeding

explanation: Spot on! A firm, contracted uterus clamps down on blood vessels so the mum doesn't bleed too much.

question: Which drug is commonly used first when a mother has postpartum hemorrhage from a soft uterus?

options.A: Insulin
options.B: Paracetamol
options.C: Oxytocin
options.D: Furosemide

explanation: You got it! Oxytocin helps the uterine muscle contract strongly to stop heavy bleeding.

question: Ten minutes after delivery, a mum starts bleeding heavily and her uterus feels soft and boggy. What should you do right away?

options.A: Encourage the mother to walk around the room to boost circulation
options.B: Wait patiently for thirty minutes to see if the bleeding stops on its own
options.C: Send the patient home immediately with iron tablets
options.D: Perform fundal massage and administer the prescribed uterotonic drug

explanation: Well done! Massaging the uterus helps it contract, and giving the uterotonic medication stops the bleeding fast.

question: What important document must go with a patient when transferring her from a maternity home to a bigger hospital?

options.A: A clear and detailed referral note
options.B: A signed financial guarantee form
options.C: An inventory list of delivery room tools
options.D: A copy of the facility tax clearance certificate

explanation: Correct! The referral note tells the receiving team what has happened so far and what care she needs.

question: Why are fast transport and clear communication so vital during a maternity emergency referral?

options.A: It allows the receiving hospital to prepare a private room
options.B: It prevents dangerous delays in treating life-threatening complications
options.C: It reduces the administrative paperwork for the nursing staff
options.D: It ensures the maternity home gets a refund for medical supplies

explanation: Spot on! Every minute counts in an emergency, and cutting down delays saves lives.

question: What is the single most effective way to stop infections from spreading between patients in a ward?

options.A: Closing the windows to keep outdoor dust away
options.B: Consistent and proper hand hygiene by all staff
options.C: Burning all hospital bedsheets after a single use
options.D: Using scented air fresheners in the delivery room

explanation: You nailed it! Good hand hygiene is the number one defense against hospital-acquired infections.

question: Why do maternity homes hold clinical audits and review close-calls?

options.A: To find staff members to penalize for minor mistakes
options.B: To increase the cost of antenatal registration fees
options.C: To identify safety gaps and improve future clinical care quality
options.D: To reduce the number of patients seeking care at the facility

explanation: That's right! Audits help the team learn from close-calls so they can make patient care safer for the next mum.

question: What is the main focus of long-term care compared to acute care?

options.A: Performing emergency procedures and trauma resuscitation
options.B: Providing short-term surgical recovery and rapid discharge
options.C: Maintaining quality of life and managing chronic conditions
options.D: Curing acute infections and stabilizing vital signs

explanation: You've got this! While acute care focuses on sudden illnesses, long-term care is all about steady, ongoing support and helping people live well with long-standing health challenges.

question: Which group makes up most of the residents in long-term care facilities?

options.A: Adults admitted strictly for acute post-surgical wound care
options.B: Children with congenital respiratory complications
options.C: Younger adults recovering from short-term sports injuries
options.D: Older adults with multiple chronic illnesses and frailty

explanation: Spot on! Older adults make up the majority of long-term care residents because aging often brings multiple health needs that require daily support.

question: What is the primary goal of long-term care?

options.A: Restricting resident autonomy to maintain strict institutional rules
options.B: Ensuring rapid patient discharge within seventy-two hours
options.C: Completely reversing all chronic disease processes
options.D: Promoting the highest possible level of well-being and independence

explanation: Great thinking! Long-term care isn't about a quick cure; it's about helping residents stay as independent and happy as possible every single day.

question: Why is allowing residents to make their own choices (autonomy) so important in long-term care?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any nursing staff supervision
options.B: It accelerates the natural healing of acute infections
options.C: It helps preserve resident dignity and psychological health
options.D: It reduces the financial cost of running the facility

explanation: Spot on! When people can still make choices about their day, it boosts their self-worth and keeps their spirits high.

question: In nursing, what does the common acronym ADL stand for?

options.A: Advanced Dietary List
options.B: Alternate Drug Logistics
options.C: Activities of Daily Living
options.D: Acute Disease Level

explanation: You nailed it! ADLs are the everyday things we do to care for ourselves, like bathing, dressing, and eating.

question: A resident needs physical help to cut their food and bring it to their mouth. Which daily living activity does this fall under?

options.A: Bathing
options.B: Feeding
options.C: Transferring
options.D: Toileting

explanation: Well done! Eating and drinking assistance is classified under the feeding category of ADLs.

question: What is the main idea behind person-centered care planning?

options.A: Allowing the nursing staff to make all daily decisions without input
options.B: Focusing solely on medical diagnoses while ignoring social history
options.C: Enforcing a strict morning schedule that all residents must follow
options.D: Tailoring care around the individual preferences and past routines of the resident

explanation: Exactly right! Person-centered care treats the resident as a unique human being, honoring their personal history and everyday preferences.

question: Which of the following is a common positive result of using person-centered care?

options.A: Decreased staffing requirements across all shifts
options.B: Shorter hospital stays for acute trauma patients
options.C: Reduced behavioral symptoms in residents with dementia
options.D: Elimination of the need for any medication administration

explanation: Spot on! When patients feel heard, respected, and comfortable, it often lowers anxiety and reduces challenging behaviors in dementia.

question: Which healthcare team members usually spend the most time providing direct, hands-on daily care to residents?

options.A: Certified Nursing Assistants
options.B: Physician specialists
options.C: Registered Dietitians
options.D: Hospital administrators

explanation: You got it! CNAs are the bedside backbone of long-term care, spending the most hours helping residents with daily needs.

question: Why is teamwork among different healthcare professionals so crucial in long-term care?

options.A: Medical doctors require assistance to perform basic personal hygiene
options.B: Residents typically have multiple complex physical, emotional, and social needs
options.C: It ensures that nurses never have to communicate with resident families
options.D: It removes the need for documenting resident care assessments

explanation: Brilliant! Because residents have varied needs, nurses, doctors, dietitians, and therapists must work hand-in-hand to cover all bases.

question: What is a key nursing action to prevent bedsores (pressure injuries) in immobile residents?

options.A: Applying strong antiseptic ointment to all bony areas
options.B: Limiting fluid intake to prevent skin moisture
options.C: Keeping the resident in bed twenty-four hours a day
options.D: Implementing regular repositioning schedules

explanation: Spot on! Turning and repositioning patients regularly takes the weight off bony spots, keeping their skin safe and healthy.

question: A nurse notices an unsteady resident pacing near a cluttered hallway. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Administer a strong sedative medication to keep the resident asleep
options.B: Ignore the situation since walking independently is always encouraged
options.C: Clear the hallway clutter and assist the resident safely back to their seat
options.D: Instruct the resident to run down the hallway to improve agility

explanation: You've got it! Clearing out obstacles right away is a quick, life-saving step to prevent falls.

question: What is the main purpose of advance directives in long-term care?

options.A: To outline a resident's treatment preferences before they lose decision-making capacity
options.B: To schedule mandatory physical therapy sessions for new admissions
options.C: To determine the monthly financial billing rates for facility room and board
options.D: To assign nursing shift schedules for the upcoming week

explanation: Spot on! Advance directives let people speak for themselves ahead of time about the medical care they want if they ever become unable to decide.

question: How does palliative care differ from curative care when dealing with advanced chronic illness?

options.A: Palliative care eliminates the need for any nursing or medical supervision
options.B: Palliative care focuses exclusively on performing emergency surgical procedures
options.C: Palliative care prioritizes comfort, pain control, and quality of life over curing the disease
options.D: Palliative care is only provided to patients admitted for short-term rehabilitation

explanation: Great job! When a disease can no longer be cured, palliative care shifts the focus entirely to keeping the patient comfortable, peaceful, and pain-free.

question: What is the main difference between skilled care and custodial care?

options.A: Skilled care requires licensed health professionals for complex medical needs.
options.B: Custodial care is only provided inside large acute care hospitals.
options.C: Custodial care requires advanced clinical judgment and monitoring.
options.D: Skilled care focuses exclusively on helping residents bathe and dress.

explanation: You've got this! Skilled care is all about medical tasks done by trained pros, while custodial care helps with everyday living activities like bathing. Great job keeping them straight!

question: Why is skilled care so important for an elderly patient just leaving the hospital?

options.A: To replace the need for any future primary care physician visits.
options.B: To prevent minor clinical changes from turning into severe health emergencies.
options.C: To ensure the patient never returns to their personal home.
options.D: To completely eliminate all forms of physical therapy.

explanation: Spotting small health changes early is what skilled nursing is all about! It keeps our patients stable and out of trouble. Well done!

question: What is a major goal of skilled care when looking after someone with a long-term, chronic illness?

options.A: Elimination of all daily living assistance needs.
options.B: Complete permanent cure of the underlying disease.
options.C: Immediate discharge back to independent living.
options.D: Stabilization, symptom relief, and functional preservation.

explanation: When a chronic condition can't be cured, our goal shifts to keeping the patient comfortable, managing symptoms, and helping them stay as active as possible.

question: Why must nurses balance medical treatments with a resident's personal wishes?

options.A: To avoid documenting any clinical changes in the chart.
options.B: To ensure the patient performs all physical therapy alone.
options.C: To respect resident dignity while still achieving safe, effective outcomes.
options.D: To completely bypass hospital discharge regulations.

explanation: Person-centered care means we team up with our patients, respecting what they value while keeping them safe and healthy. You're doing great!

question: Which of these nursing duties counts as a skilled nursing intervention?

options.A: Managing complex wound care and dressing changes.
options.B: Assisting a resident with walking down the hallway.
options.C: Handing out meal trays to all residents at lunchtime.
options.D: Helping a resident put on their casual daytime clothes.

explanation: Wound care needs professional clinical technique and assessment, making it a true skilled nursing task!

question: A patient with a new tracheostomy needs airway suctioning. Why is this considered skilled care?

options.A: It is a basic personal hygiene task that any family member can perform.
options.B: It replaces the need for daily medication administration.
options.C: It is only performed once a year during an annual physical exam.
options.D: It requires specialized clinical knowledge to prevent airway occlusion and infection.

explanation: Keeping an airway clear takes specialized training and sharp monitoring to stop dangerous complications like breathing trouble. Excellent work!

question: What is the main job of the registered nurse inside a healthcare team?

options.A: Replacing the dietician for meal planning and kitchen duties.
options.B: Providing all physical therapy exercises without therapist assistance.
options.C: Prescribing new medications when the doctor is off duty.
options.D: Acting as the clinical hub to coordinate care among all disciplines.

explanation: As nurses, we bring the whole healthcare team together so everyone is on the same page for the patient's care. You're mastering teamwork!

question: Why is teamwork among different health professionals so vital in a nursing facility?

options.A: It prevents fragmented care and addresses the resident's total health needs.
options.B: It reduces the total number of staff required on every shift.
options.C: It allows nurses to avoid communicating directly with resident families.
options.D: It eliminates the need for any written nursing documentation.

explanation: When doctors, nurses, therapists, and dieticians work hand in hand, nothing falls through the cracks for the resident.

question: What tool is commonly used in skilled care settings to assess and track resident health status?

options.A: Minimum Data Set (MDS)
options.B: Pediatric growth chart
options.C: Surgical safety checklist
options.D: Emergency room triage scale

explanation: The Minimum Data Set (MDS) is a standard assessment tool used in long-term care facilities to evaluate how a resident is doing.

question: Why do we say a resident's care plan must be treated as a living document?

options.A: It is legally required to be rewritten word-for-word every single morning.
options.B: It is only used during the initial admission interview and never again.
options.C: It must be adjusted whenever the resident's clinical condition changes.
options.D: It prevents nurses from having to document daily shift assessments.

explanation: A resident's health changes day by day, so their care plan needs to grow and update right along with them. Spot on!

question: Why must nurses watch out for medication build-up in older adults receiving skilled care?

options.A: Renal and hepatic function always improve with advanced age.
options.B: Decreased kidney and liver function can lead to drug accumulation and toxicity.
options.C: Older adults process all drugs much faster than younger adults do.
options.D: Medications have no side effects once a patient enters a nursing home.

explanation: As the body ages, the kidneys and liver naturally slow down a bit. This means drugs stay in the system longer, so we have to watch for toxic build-up. Brilliant thinking!

question: An older resident taking blood pressure pills suddenly feels dizzy and takes a fall. What should the nurse think of first?

options.A: An immediate need to discharge the resident home.
options.B: The complete absence of any pharmacological influence.
options.C: A normal reaction that requires no clinical follow-up.
options.D: A potential adverse drug reaction or cumulative medication effect.

explanation: Dizziness and sudden falls in older adults are classic clues that a medication might be lowering their blood pressure too much or making them drowsy.

question: What is the main goal of restorative nursing programs in skilled facilities?

options.A: To maintain functional gains achieved during formal therapy sessions.
options.B: To provide custodial care without any medical oversight.
options.C: To replace physical therapists entirely for every resident.
options.D: To eliminate all physical activity for frail residents.

explanation: Restorative care helps residents practice what they learned in therapy so they don't lose their hard-earned progress!

question: Why should nurses encourage residents to do tasks for themselves whenever they can?

options.A: To punish residents who refuse to participate in group activities.
options.B: To allow nursing staff to take longer breaks during the day.
options.C: To prevent rapid physical deconditioning and preserve independence.
options.D: To reduce the total amount of paperwork required for the shift.

explanation: Encouraging self-care keeps muscles strong and helps residents hold onto their independence and confidence. You're thinking like a real nurse!

question: Why is clear, objective nursing documentation so crucial in skilled care facilities?

options.A: It is only used by insurance companies to deny resident coverage.
options.B: It guarantees that no resident will ever experience a fall.
options.C: It serves as a legal safeguard and proves that skilled criteria were met.
options.D: It replaces the need for verbal shift handovers between nurses.

explanation: Good charting is your best friend! It acts as a legal proof that the resident truly needed and received expert nursing care.

question: How do quality improvement teams use data like fall rates and skin injury reports?

options.A: To hide negative clinical outcomes from state regulatory agencies.
options.B: To track performance trends and guide system-wide safety improvements.
options.C: To find individual nurses to blame whenever an accident happens.
options.D: To determine which residents should be discharged immediately.

explanation: Quality improvement isn't about blaming people—it's about spotting trends so we can make our hospital or facility safer for everyone!

question: What is the main focus of custodial care?

options.A: Performing emergency surgeries and acute trauma procedures
options.B: Administering complex intravenous medications and therapies
options.C: Providing non-medical help with daily living and personal needs
options.D: Curing acute infections through targeted antibiotic therapy

explanation: Custodial care is entirely non-medical and centers on helping people manage their routine daily needs rather than curing active diseases. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h1)

question: Who is most likely to require custodial care over a long period?

options.A: An athlete recovering from a simple sports-related ankle sprain
options.B: A patient with a sudden bacterial infection needing a short antibiotic course
options.C: A person admitted to the emergency ward with acute appendicitis
options.D: An individual with chronic physical disabilities or severe cognitive loss

explanation: People with chronic disabilities or long-term cognitive decline often lose the ability to care for themselves independently, making custodial support necessary. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h1)

question: What does the acronym ADL stand for in healthcare?

options.A: Advanced Drug List
options.B: Activities of Daily Living
options.C: Assisted Diet Limitation
options.D: Acute Disease Level

explanation: ADLs stand for Activities of Daily Living, which represent the essential self-care tasks required every day. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h2)

question: A caregiver helps a frail elderly client move safely from a wheelchair onto the living room sofa. Which specific ADL is this caregiver assisting with?

options.A: Feeding
options.B: Dressing
options.C: Bathing
options.D: Transferring

explanation: Moving a patient between surfaces, such as from a bed to a chair or wheelchair to a sofa, falls under the category of transferring. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h2)

question: Why is custodial care considered different from skilled nursing care?

options.A: Skilled nursing care is strictly limited to helping patients eat meals.
options.B: Custodial care focuses on non-medical daily support rather than clinical treatments.
options.C: Custodial care can only be performed inside a licensed intensive care unit.
options.D: Skilled nursing care does not require any form of professional training.

explanation: Custodial care is meant for daily personal tasks, whereas skilled nursing involves medical procedures ordered by a physician and performed by licensed nurses. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h3)

question: Which of the following interventions requires skilled nursing rather than basic custodial care?

options.A: Helping a client put on a shirt and button up the front
options.B: Walking beside an elderly client to prevent a fall in the hallway
options.C: Cutting meat into small pieces on a plate during lunch
options.D: Changing a complex surgical wound dressing and monitoring an IV line

explanation: Wound dressings and intravenous lines are clinical medical procedures that require the expertise of a skilled nurse. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h3)

question: What is caregiver burnout?

options.A: An allergic reaction to cleaning supplies used in the home
options.B: Physical and emotional exhaustion caused by prolonged caregiving stress
options.C: A sudden medical illness caught from a patient in the hospital
options.D: The legal termination of a home health care contract

explanation: Caregiver burnout happens when family or informal caregivers become overwhelmed by the continuous physical and emotional demands of supporting a relative. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h4)

question: How do nursing assistants contribute to the healthcare team during custodial care?

options.A: They prescribe complex pharmacological drugs and diagnose medical diseases.
options.B: They perform major surgical procedures in home environments.
options.C: They observe daily changes in the client and report them to professional nurses.
options.D: They handle hospital finance bills and insurance policies.

explanation: While nursing assistants do not diagnose or treat, they spend the most time with clients and serve as vital observers who report new symptoms or changes. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h4)

question: Which environmental hazard is most commonly removed to prevent falls in a home care setting?

options.A: Solid dining tables
options.B: Heavy wooden wardrobes
options.C: Loose scatter rugs
options.D: Ceiling light fixtures

explanation: Loose rugs easily slip underfoot or catch walking aids, making them a major hazard for elderly clients with poor balance. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h5)

question: An elderly client with limited mobility spends most of the day lying in bed. What is the most important preventive action the caregiver should take?

options.A: Leave the client alone for long hours to promote independence
options.B: Keep the bedroom completely dark to encourage deep sleep
options.C: Reposition the client frequently to protect skin integrity
options.D: Restrict all fluid intake to prevent bathroom accidents

explanation: Regular turning and repositioning relieve pressure on bony areas, which is critical for preventing painful pressure ulcers in bedbound clients. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h5)

question: How is custodial care traditionally provided in most Nigerian communities?

options.A: Exclusively through government-funded nursing homes
options.B: By international insurance companies paying for home aides
options.C: Through mandatory hospital stays for all elderly citizens
options.D: Through extended family networks and shared family duty

explanation: Nigerian culture traditionally relies on the extended family system to care for aging or disabled relatives at home. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h6)

question: What is a major challenge facing families who seek formal custodial care in urban Nigerian cities?

options.A: High out-of-pocket costs because insurance rarely covers non-medical care
options.B: Strict government laws that forbid hiring private home caregivers
options.C: Complete lack of any individuals willing to work as caregivers
options.D: An overabundance of free public nursing homes in every neighborhood

explanation: Because health insurance typically covers acute medical care rather than long-term custodial help, families must pay out of pocket for private aides. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T4#GNS324_U5_T4_h6)

question: What was the main purpose of early almshouses and poorhouses?

options.A: To provide advanced surgical and medical treatments
options.B: To train the first generation of registered nurses
options.C: To serve as specialized retirement homes for the wealthy
options.D: To shelter the destitute, elderly, and chronically ill

explanation: Think of early almshouses as general community shelters. They were set up to care for people who had no one else, like the poor and frail elderly, long before modern hospitals and nursing homes existed!

question: Why were early almshouses poorly suited for caring for the sick and elderly?

options.A: They suffered from severe overcrowding and a lack of medical staff
options.B: They charged fees that only wealthy families could afford
options.C: They focused too heavily on expensive experimental therapies
options.D: They refused to admit anyone over the age of fifty

explanation: These places were often jam-packed and lacked trained health workers. Mixing different vulnerable people together without proper medical care meant chronic illnesses weren't managed well.

question: Which post-WWII law provided funding for hospital construction and indirectly led to the growth of nursing homes?

options.A: The Social Security Amendment
options.B: The Medicare and Medicaid Act
options.C: The Nursing Home Reform Act
options.D: The Hill-Burton Act

explanation: The Hill-Burton Act funded a massive wave of hospital building. Once those hospitals started discharging patients who still needed long-term care, the need for separate nursing homes became super obvious!

question: How did the post-WWII era change the main reason why nursing homes were opened?

options.A: Religious organizations closed all facilities to focus solely on home nursing
options.B: Communities stopped caring for older adults outside of acute hospitals
options.C: Governments took direct control of all private health institutions
options.D: Eldercare shifted from a charitable or public welfare function into a commercial business

explanation: With hospitals discharging more chronically ill older adults, private business owners saw a chance to step in and turn eldercare into a profitable commercial venture.

question: Which government program became the main payer for long-term nursing home care after 1965?

options.A: Medicare
options.B: The Hill-Burton fund
options.C: Social Security
options.D: Medicaid

explanation: Medicaid was built to support low-income individuals, and over time it grew to become the primary financial backbone paying for long-term stays in nursing facilities.

question: A newly opened nursing home focuses entirely on packing in as many residents as possible to maximize government payouts. Based on trends from the 1960s and 70s, what is a likely result?

options.A: Excessive funding directly spent on recreational programs
options.B: Compromised quality of resident care and severe staff burnout
options.C: Immediate elimination of all chronic health conditions
options.D: Universal praise from visiting public health inspectors

explanation: When a facility chases high numbers over quality care, they usually cut corners on staffing. This leaves nurses overworked and patients getting less-than-ideal attention.

question: What major change did the Nursing Home Reform Act of 1987 introduce regarding resident management?

options.A: It removed all requirements for regular state health inspections
options.B: It placed severe restrictions on the use of physical and chemical restraints
options.C: It encouraged facilities to lock residents in rooms for safety
options.D: It mandated that all residents must take daily sedative medications

explanation: The 1987 law stepped in because restraints were often used just to make life easier for staff rather than keeping patients safe. The law heavily cracked down on this practice!

question: Why was the Minimum Data Set (MDS) introduced as part of the 1987 reforms?

options.A: To determine which staff members should be terminated each quarter
options.B: To standardize comprehensive resident assessments and guide individualized care planning
options.C: To calculate the exact profit margins for private facility owners
options.D: To track how many visitors each resident received every week

explanation: The MDS is a fantastic tool for nurses! It ensures every resident gets a thorough health assessment so the team can build a care plan tailored specifically to that person's needs.

question: What is the primary goal of person-centered care in modern long-term facilities?

options.A: To honor individual resident preferences, choices, and daily routines
options.B: To reduce operating costs by standardizing all resident meals
options.C: To enforce strict schedules that make facility operations more efficient
options.D: To eliminate the need for any licensed nursing staff on site

explanation: Person-centered care puts the resident first! Instead of forcing everyone onto a rigid hospital schedule, it revolves around what the individual patient actually likes and prefers.

question: How does assisted living differ fundamentally from traditional skilled nursing homes?

options.A: It provides a homelike environment that emphasizes autonomy and help with daily tasks rather than heavy medical care
options.B: It relies entirely on family members to provide all professional nursing services
options.C: It refuses admission to any older adult who has a chronic medical condition
options.D: It operates strictly as a hospital ward for patients requiring mechanical ventilation

explanation: Assisted living is meant for folks who just need a little boost with daily activities (like bathing or dressing) but don't need round-the-clock intensive medical nursing.

question: What is a major workforce challenge currently facing the long-term care industry?

options.A: An overabundance of licensed nurses competing for very few open beds
options.B: Mandatory retirement ages that force nurses to leave the field early
options.C: Severe staff shortages and high burnout rates among nurses and aides
options.D: Strict laws prohibiting nurses from working in residential settings

explanation: It's no secret that long-term care can be tough. Low pay, heavy workloads, and physical demands mean keeping and recruiting enough nurses remains a major hurdle.

question: What is the main purpose of innovative 'small-house' models in modern nursing care?

options.A: To eliminate the need for any professional healthcare oversight
options.B: To lower building construction costs by using temporary tents
options.C: To break large, sterile institutions down into homelike residential units
options.D: To reduce the total number of older adults requiring assistance worldwide

explanation: Small-house models ditch the long, intimidating hospital hallways and replace them with cozy, home-style spaces where residents can build genuine community connections.

question: What is the main purpose of an assisted living facility?

options.A: Serving as a permanent substitute for acute hospital stays
options.B: Housing only individuals with severe mental health disorders
options.C: Providing support for daily tasks while keeping independence
options.D: Offering around-the-clock intensive medical and surgical care

explanation: Assisted living is designed for people who need some help with daily living but do not require heavy nursing care, allowing them to remain as independent as possible. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T6#GNS324_U5_T6_h1)

question: How do assisted living facilities differ from traditional nursing homes?

options.A: Assisted living requires continuous 24-hour physician supervision.
options.B: Nursing homes provide much less medical oversight than assisted living.
options.C: Nursing homes only admit individuals who are completely independent.
options.D: Assisted living focuses more on a home-like setting and independence.

explanation: While nursing homes offer heavy, continuous medical and nursing care, assisted living emphasizes residential comfort and autonomy with lesser medical intervention. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T6#GNS324_U5_T6_h1)

question: What is evaluated during a functional assessment prior to admission?

options.A: Financial credit history
options.B: Workplace performance record
options.C: Previous travel experiences
options.D: Activities of daily living

explanation: A functional assessment looks closely at how well a potential resident can manage basic daily self-care tasks like bathing and dressing. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T6#GNS324_U5_T6_h2)

question: A client with advanced dementia who wanders at night is being checked into an assisted living facility that does not have a secure memory unit. What should the facility do?

options.A: Wait until the client's memory improves on its own
options.B: Deny admission because the facility cannot keep the client safe
options.C: Admit the client and just use door chimes for night safety
options.D: Accept the client and assign a private nurse paid by the family

explanation: You've got this! Facilities must match their care to what the client genuinely needs. Admitting a wandering client to an unsecure place creates a big safety risk.

question: Which service is typically included as a core offering in an assisted living facility?

options.A: Complex intravenous chemotherapy administration
options.B: Intensive care unit mechanical ventilation
options.C: Major orthopedic surgical procedures
options.D: Assistance with daily personal hygiene and bathing

explanation: Personal care assistance with hygiene, dressing, and bathing forms the core foundation of daily services in assisted living. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T6#GNS324_U5_T6_h3)

question: Why do care staff encourage residents to do parts of their morning routine all by themselves?

options.A: To reduce the total number of staff members needed on duty
options.B: To eliminate the need for any individualized service plans
options.C: To comply with federal acute care hospital regulations
options.D: To prevent physical decline caused by lack of use

explanation: Great thinking! Letting residents do what they can manage preserves their muscle strength, coordination, and sense of pride.

question: What is a primary responsibility of a nurse working in an assisted living facility?

options.A: Managing hospital emergency room admissions
options.B: Monitoring health status and coordinating care services
options.C: Running the facility financial and accounting department
options.D: Performing major surgical operations on-site

explanation: Assisted living nurses focus on health monitoring, wellness checks, and coordinating various support and medical services for the residents. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T6#GNS324_U5_T6_h4)

question: How is the role of a nurse in assisted living different from a nurse in a busy hospital?

options.A: Assisted living nurses focus more on wellness, supervision, and chronic care coordination.
options.B: Acute care nurses have no responsibility for monitoring patient vital signs.
options.C: Assisted living nurses provide continuous one-on-one surgical recovery care.
options.D: Acute care nurses never supervise nursing assistants.

explanation: Spot on! While hospital nurses handle unstable, emergency conditions, assisted living nurses focus on long-term wellness, chronic care, and guiding support staff.

question: What is the document used by staff to track when medications are given to residents?

options.A: Maintenance repair schedule
options.B: Medication administration record
options.C: Facility financial balance sheet
options.D: Daily dietary menu log

explanation: The medication administration record, or MAR, is the official document used to track every dose of medication given to a resident. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T6#GNS324_U5_T6_h5)

question: A resident says they already took their morning blood pressure pill, but the medication administration record (MAR) is blank for that time. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Administer a second dose immediately to ensure their blood pressure stays controlled
options.B: Wait until the evening shift to see if the blood pressure spikes
options.C: Assume the resident is correct and sign the record as given by the resident
options.D: Withhold the dose and consult the prescribing physician or charge nurse before acting

explanation: Brilliant! Giving a double dose can be dangerous. Always pause, check the facts, and consult your senior colleagues or doctor when something doesn't match up.

question: What is a key benefit of offering structured social activities in assisted living?

options.A: Replacing the need for family visits altogether
options.B: Reducing the cost of building maintenance
options.C: Combating feelings of loneliness and depression
options.D: Eliminating the need for any routine medical care

explanation: Group activities and social events help keep residents engaged, active, and emotionally connected, reducing isolation and depression. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T6#GNS324_U5_T6_h6)

question: Why is it important for assisted living homes to balance safety rules with personal freedom?

options.A: Residents who experience freedom no longer require medical care.
options.B: Federal laws prohibit any facility from locking doors or windows.
options.C: Excessive rules can strip away a resident's dignity and sense of home.
options.D: Safety protocols have no impact on the mental health of older adults.

explanation: You've got this! Safety matters, but making a home feel like a strict prison hurts residents' happiness and takes away their independence.

question: Which government body is mainly responsible for inspecting and licensing assisted living facilities?

options.A: State health or social services departments
options.B: Federal military defense agencies
options.C: International travel and tourism boards
options.D: National automotive safety councils

explanation: State health departments set the rules, run routine checks, and make sure assisted living homes follow health and safety laws.

question: What must an assisted living facility do after inspectors find a safety or rule violation during a visit?

options.A: Submit and implement a formal plan of correction
options.B: Immediately close the building and relocate all residents
options.C: Change the state laws to match current facility practices
options.D: Ignore the finding if staff members disagree with it

explanation: Spot on! When inspectors find a problem, the facility has to write down a clear plan showing how they will fix it and make sure it never happens again.

question: What is the primary purpose of an adult day care home?

options.A: To offer permanent residential housing for older adults
options.B: To serve as a 24-hour acute care hospital ward
options.C: To provide specialized surgical interventions
options.D: To provide daytime supervised care and support services

explanation: Adult day care homes are specifically designed to offer structured programs, supervision, and support during daytime hours while allowing clients to return home at night. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h1)

question: How do adult day care homes primarily benefit family caregivers?

options.A: By taking over complete legal and financial responsibility for the client
options.B: By training family members to become licensed practical nurses
options.C: By permanently removing the need for any home-based care
options.D: By offering temporary respite to prevent physical and emotional burnout

explanation: These facilities give family caregivers a necessary break from constant responsibilities, helping them sustain their own health and continue working or managing personal tasks. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h1)

question: Which model of adult day care focuses primarily on meals, recreation, and socialization without intensive health services?

options.A: Surgical model
options.B: Social model
options.C: Acute care model
options.D: Medical model

explanation: The social model is centered around community interaction, leisure activities, and basic supervision rather than active medical treatments. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h2)

question: A client with advanced Alzheimer's disease who wanders needs a secure environment with specialized cognitive programs. Which facility type is most appropriate?

options.A: Standard social model center
options.B: Acute psychiatric ward
options.C: Outpatient physical therapy clinic
options.D: Specialized model adult day center

explanation: Specialized models cater to specific groups like dementia patients, providing the required secure environments and targeted cognitive stimulation. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h2)

question: What is a common inclusion criterion for admission to an adult day care home?

options.A: Mild to moderate functional decline requiring daytime supervision
options.B: Requirement for round-the-clock intensive surgical nursing
options.C: Comatose state requiring mechanical ventilation
options.D: Active and untreated infectious respiratory disease

explanation: Clients who need structured daytime support, socialization, or supervision while remaining at home at night are prime candidates for day care. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h3)

question: Which condition would most likely lead to a client being denied admission to a standard adult day care center?

options.A: Using a walker or cane for safe indoor mobility
options.B: Needing assistance with eating meals during the day
options.C: Mild forgetfulness associated with early-stage aging
options.D: Severe, unpredictable physical aggression toward others

explanation: Uncontrolled aggressive behaviors pose safety risks to staff and other participants, making standard day care settings unsuitable unless specialized behavioral resources exist. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h3)

question: What is the primary goal of conducting regular nursing assessments in an adult day care setting?

options.A: To establish health baselines and catch subtle changes early
options.B: To enforce strict institutional rules upon the clients
options.C: To diagnose complex mental health disorders independently
options.D: To permanently replace the client's primary care physician

explanation: Regular assessments help nurses monitor chronic conditions and identify early signs of physical or cognitive deterioration before they become acute emergencies. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h4)

question: Why does a comprehensive assessment in day care include evaluating the family caregiver?

options.A: To legally transfer family financial assets to the facility
options.B: To determine if the caregiver has a valid nursing license
options.C: To replace family involvement entirely with facility staff
options.D: To gauge caregiver stress and the sustainability of home care

explanation: Understanding caregiver strain helps the nursing team provide proper support and respite services, ensuring the client can safely remain at home. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h4)

question: How should therapeutic activities in adult day care be viewed?

options.A: As optional events that have no real health benefits
options.B: As purposeful interventions to enhance physical and cognitive well-being
options.C: As mandatory physical punishment for uncooperative behavior
options.D: As simple distractions to keep clients quiet until closing time

explanation: Activities are carefully chosen therapeutic tools designed to maintain mobility, stimulate memory, and promote social connection. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h5)

question: An activity coordinator plans a group exercise session. Which client adaptation best demonstrates person-centered care?

options.A: Excusing clients from participating if they look tired once
options.B: Requiring all clients to stand and follow the exact same routine
options.C: Skipping physical exercise altogether for safety reasons
options.D: Providing seated chair exercises for clients with poor balance

explanation: Adapting activities to individual functional levels, such as offering seated options, ensures safe and inclusive participation for everyone. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h5)

question: What is a key nursing responsibility regarding medication management in adult day care?

options.A: Prescribing new medications whenever a client reports mild discomfort
options.B: Manufacturing custom pharmaceutical compounds on-site for each client
options.C: Allowing clients to share their prescription drugs freely among peers
options.D: Verifying orders, administering or supervising intake, and monitoring for side effects

explanation: Nurses ensure medication safety by checking dosages, administering or supervising consumption, and watching closely for adverse reactions. [learn more](GNS324_U5_T7#GNS324_U5_T7_h6)
